# 🗺️ Locality Research Guide: County Cork, Ireland — 1830s–1840s

**Jurisdiction:** Cork, Munster, Ireland (county in existence since 1606; also note Cork City as a separate sub-jurisdiction)
**Period surveyed:** c. 1820–1860 (broadened slightly to capture run-up and run-out context)
**Wiki source:** [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy)

---

## ⚠️ Critical Context: Two Major Record Losses

Before surveying individual record types, you must understand two catastrophes that shape all Cork research:

1. **1922 Four Courts Fire** — The Public Record Office of Ireland was destroyed during the Irish Civil War. Most pre-1901 census returns and vast quantities of wills, government records, and other centrally-held documents were lost. This is the defining obstacle in pre-Famine Irish research.
2. **The Great Famine (1845–1852)** — Your ancestor emigrated during or just before/during this period. Famine mortality, migration, and social disruption mean that family units were often broken up or wiped out, and local record-keeping was disrupted.

---

## 1. Civil Registration — ❌ NOT AVAILABLE for Target Period

| Record type | Registration began | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Births & deaths | **1 January 1864** | No civil certificates exist for the 1830s–1840s |
| RC marriages | **1 January 1864** | Likewise absent |
| Non-Catholic marriages | **1845** | Church of Ireland, Presbyterian, Quaker marriages registered from 1845 onward |

**Action:** For births, deaths, and Catholic marriages in the 1830s–1840s, you must use **church registers** (below) — there are no civil records to find.

---

## 2. Church Records — ⭐ PRIMARY SOURCE for the Period

The FamilySearch Wiki identifies RC parish registers as the **core source** for Catholic families in this period.

### Roman Catholic Registers
- **Content:** Baptisms (births) and marriages; burials are rare
- **Cork coverage:** Many Cork parishes have registers beginning in the **1810s–1830s**, putting your target decade squarely within reach — though survival varies widely parish by parish
- **Where held:** The **National Library of Ireland (NLI)** holds microfilm and digital images of RC registers up to 1880, available **free online** at [registers.nli.ie](https://registers.nli.ie)
- **Access level:** Digital images online; indexing varies by parish

### Church of Ireland (Anglican) Registers
- **Content:** Baptisms, marriages, burials
- **Where held:** The **Representative Church Body Library (RCBL)**, Dublin; some remain in local parish custody
- **Note:** Pre-Famine CoI registers for Cork exist for many parishes but coverage is uneven after the 1922 fire destroyed some copies

### Presbyterian, Methodist, Quaker Registers
- If your ancestor was non-Catholic, consult the **Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI)** and denominational archives. Quaker registers for Munster are relatively well-preserved.

**Key quirk:** Always identify the **civil parish** your ancestor was likely in before searching — RC parishes do not follow civil parish boundaries, and one townland might fall under a different RC parish than the one you assume.

---

## 3. Census Substitutes — ⭐ ESSENTIAL (Actual Census Returns Destroyed)

The 1841 and 1851 census returns for Cork were destroyed in 1922. Two substitutes are the backbone of 1830s–1850s Cork research:

### Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837)
- **What they are:** Tax surveys listing occupiers of tithe-liable agricultural land, compiled townland by townland
- **Coverage for target period:** Directly covers the **1820s–1830s** — the earliest of your two decades
- **Who is included:** Male heads of household on agricultural land (not landless labourers, urban dwellers, or very small cottiers in many cases)
- **Where held / online:** Free online at [IrishGenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie) and [FamilySearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org); also on Ancestry
- **Access level:** Indexed and searchable online

### Griffith's Valuation (published for Cork c. early 1850s)
- **What it is:** A comprehensive property survey listing every householder (including cottiers and small tenants) with the name of the property owner
- **Coverage for target period:** Published just after your window (early 1850s) but captures the generation that lived through the 1840s; extremely useful as a "where did the family live?" anchor
- **Who is included:** Far broader than the Tithe Books — landless labourers with even a cabin are often listed
- **Where held / online:** Free at [AskAboutIreland.ie](https://www.askaboutireland.ie/griffith-valuation/) and on [Ancestry](https://www.ancestry.com); also at [IrishGenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie)
- **Access level:** Indexed and searchable online

**Use together:** Cross-reference the Tithe Books (1830s) and Griffith's (1850s) to track a family across the Famine decade and identify which individuals disappeared (emigrated or died).

---

## 4. Land Records

Beyond the two major surveys above, additional land records exist:

### Estate Papers
- Many Cork families were tenants on large Anglo-Irish estates. **Estate papers** (rent rolls, tenant lists, eviction records) are held at the **National Archives of Ireland (NAI)**, the NLI, and in some private collections. These are largely un-indexed and require knowing the landlord's name.

### Registry of Deeds (Dublin, from 1708)
- Records memorials of deeds, leases, and wills. Useful for propertied families. Held at the **Registry of Deeds, Dublin**; some indexes online at [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org) and Ancestry.

---

## 5. Emigration Records — ⭐ KEY for Your Scenario

The FamilySearch Wiki specifically flags Cork as a major departure point:

- **Cork/Cobh (Queenstown)** was one of Ireland's primary emigration ports, especially during and after the Famine
- **Passenger manifests** for ships leaving Cork list complete family groups, including infants — not just heads of household
- **Where to search:**
  - US arrivals: [Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com) passenger lists; [FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org) passenger collections; [Ellis Island Foundation](https://www.libertyellisfoundation.org) (post-1892)
  - Castle Garden arrivals (1820–1892): [CastleGarden.org](https://www.castlegarden.org)
  - [FindMyPast.com](https://www.findmypast.com) has Irish emigration collections including some Cork-specific records
- **Newspaper notices:** Cork newspapers (see below) sometimes printed emigration ship notices and passenger lists

---

## 6. Wills and Probate

- Pre-1858: Probate was handled by **ecclesiastical courts** (Church of Ireland diocesan courts). Cork fell under the **Diocese of Cork and Ross** and the **Diocese of Cloyne**. Many pre-1858 wills were destroyed in 1922.
- **Surviving copies and abstracts** can be found in the **NAI** (Grant Books, Will Registers) and the **NAI's online catalog** at [nationalarchives.ie](https://www.nationalarchives.ie)
- Wills were proved only for those with property — labourers and small tenants are largely absent

---

## 7. Newspapers

- **Cork Examiner** (founded 1841) and **Cork Constitution** covered the 1840s and reported births, marriages, deaths, and emigration notices for the middle and upper classes
- Held at the **Cork City Library** and partially digitized at **Newspapers.com** and the **British Newspaper Archive** ([britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk](https://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk))
- Primarily useful for merchants, farmers, and professional families — labourers rarely appear

---

## 8. Military Records

- Irish men serving in the **British Army** would have records in the **UK National Archives (TNA), Kew** — service records, pension records, muster rolls
- **Royal Irish Constabulary (RIC)** registers (from 1816) are at the **NAI** and partially online at the **TNA**
- **Militia records** for Cork are fragmentary; some survive at the NAI

---

## 9. Other Key Sources

| Source | What it covers | Where held |
|---|---|---|
| **Catholic qualification rolls / convert rolls** | Religious identity changes | NAI |
| **Freeman's Journal / Cork newspapers** | Public notices, legal ads | Cork City Library; BNA online |
| **Poor Law Union records** (from 1838) | Paupers, workhouse admissions — critical for Famine research | NAI; Cork County Council Archives |
| **School registers** (National Schools from 1831) | Children's names, parents, religion | NAI; some online at FamilySearch |
| **Church of Ireland baptismal registers** | If ancestor converted or was CoI | RCBL, Dublin |

---

## Summary: Research Priority Order for 1830s–1840s Cork

1. **RC parish baptism/marriage registers** (NLI, free online) — your most direct vital record substitute
2. **Tithe Applotment Books** (1820s–1837) — place the family on the land
3. **Griffith's Valuation** (early 1850s) — confirm who was still there after the Famine
4. **Passenger manifests** — trace the emigration event itself
5. **Newspapers** (Cork Examiner from 1841) — for middle-class families
6. **Estate papers** — if you can identify the landlord
7. **Poor Law Union records** (from 1838) — if the family was impoverished

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What's there | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Library of Ireland (NLI)** | RC parish registers to 1880 | Free online at registers.nli.ie |
| **National Archives of Ireland (NAI)** | Census fragments, wills, estate papers, Poor Law | Online catalog; reading room Dublin |
| **Representative Church Body Library (RCBL)** | Church of Ireland registers | Dublin; appointment required |
| **Cork City and County Archives** | Local civic and Poor Law records | Cork City |
| **UK National Archives (TNA), Kew** | British Army, RIC records | Online and in-person |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Tithe Books, Griffith's, passenger lists | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com / FindMyPast.com** | Griffith's, passenger lists, newspapers | Subscription |

---

**Bottom line for your research:** The 1830s–1840s in Cork is a challenging but workable window. Civil registration did not exist yet, and the 1922 fire destroyed the census returns — but RC parish registers, the Tithe Applotment Books, Griffith's Valuation, and Famine-era passenger manifests together form a solid substitute framework. If your ancestor was Catholic (the large majority in Cork), start at the **National Library of Ireland's free register images** and pair those findings with the land surveys to anchor the family geographically before tracing the emigration voyage.

# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts — 1820–1850

## Jurisdiction

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Standard place** | Berkshire, Massachusetts, United States |
| **Type** | County |
| **Established** | 1761 (from Hampshire County) |
| **County seat** | Pittsfield |
| **Borders** | New York (west); Vermont (north); Hampshire & Franklin counties (east & northeast) |

Berkshire County was fully constituted before the target period and its boundaries were stable through 1850 — no predecessor-jurisdiction complication for this window.

---

## Vital Registration: What Existed in 1820–1850

Massachusetts has one of the richest vital-record traditions in the country. Two layers operated during your period:

- **Town-level registration (the primary layer):** Town clerks were mandated by the Massachusetts General Court to record births, marriages, and deaths **at the town level from 1639**. Every Berkshire County town should have its own register running well before 1820. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Records Overview](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial))
- **Statewide registration (begins within the period):** Statewide civil registration began in **1841** under the Secretary of State — adding a second layer for 1841–1850. Consult the [Massachusetts Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy) FamilySearch Wiki article for the full statewide coverage history.
- **No county-level vital registration exists in Massachusetts** — records are at the town, not the county, level. Search town by town.

---

## Record Types, Repositories, and Digitization

### 1. Town Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths) ⚠️ Two access tiers

**Collection (name-indexed):** FamilySearch holds *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890* (collection [2061550](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550)), which covers the 1820–1850 window and is searchable by name. This collection draws heavily on the published *Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850* series, which — per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Massachusetts Genealogy#Colonial](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial)) — covers more than 200 Massachusetts towns.

**Digitized volume (browse-only):** FamilySearch has also digitized a raw volume of **Berkshire County Town Clerk Vital and Town Records, 1761–1850** (image group 004500891, 512 images). This volume is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — it must be browsed image by image. It may contain entries not yet captured in the indexed collection.

> **Quirk:** The indexed collection and the browse-only volume cover the same period but are different products. Run both: search the indexed collection first, then browse the raw volume if you need to verify or fill gaps.

**Physical / repository holdings:**
- Original town registers remain with individual **town clerks** across Berkshire County
- Transcribed records and published *Vital Records* volumes are held at the **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)**, Boston — the largest genealogical library in the region (per FamilySearch Wiki, [Massachusetts Genealogy#Military](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Military))
- **Massachusetts Archives**, Boston, holds original colony and state records from the 1620s onward

---

### 2. Church Records (Baptisms, Marriages, Burials)

Church records are essential for this period — they fill gaps before 1841 statewide registration and often recorded events the town clerk missed.

**Collection (name-indexed):** FamilySearch *Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920* (collection [1921657](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657)) — searchable by name and spans the full target window.

**Digitized volume (browse-only):** FamilySearch has digitized **Pittsfield Congregational Church Records, 1791–1850** (image group 004500892, 274 images). This is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — browse only. Congregationalism was the dominant denomination in western Massachusetts; this is a prime source for Pittsfield-area families.

> **Quirk:** Only one church-record volume surfaced for the county in the FamilySearch volume search (Pittsfield Congregational). For other towns and denominations (Baptist, Methodist, Episcopal, Quaker), check NEHGS manuscript holdings and individual church archives directly — not all have been digitized.

---

### 3. Probate Records (Wills, Inventories, Guardianships)

FamilySearch holds *Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991* (collection [1678901](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901)), which includes the 1820–1850 window and is indexed. Berkshire County probate was administered at the **Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield**. Probate files often name all heirs, ages, and relationships — a powerful substitute or complement to missing vital entries.

---

### 4. Federal Census Records

Federal censuses were taken in **1820, 1830, 1840, and 1850** — all four fall in your window.

- **1850** is the first census to name every household member with age, birthplace, and occupation. Earlier censuses (1820–1840) name only the head of household with age-bracket tick marks for the rest.
- The **1850 Mortality Schedule** lists individuals who died in the 12 months before the census and is a direct substitute for missing death records for that year.
- Access: [Ancestry.com U.S. Federal Census Collection](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) (subscription) and FamilySearch (free).

---

### 5. Land and Deed Records

Deeds were recorded at the **county level** in Massachusetts from the 1630s — per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Massachusetts Genealogy#Colonial](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial)), Berkshire County deed books survive in remarkably complete runs. Repository: **Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield**. FamilySearch microfilm holdings should be checked via the catalog.

---

### 6. Military Records

Your period covers the **War of 1812** aftermath (pensions active through 1850s) and **Mexican-American War** service (1846–1848).

- **Pension files and bounty-land warrants** at NARA are particularly rich — they often contain birth dates, marriage affidavits, and widow's depositions with extensive family detail.
- **Massachusetts adjutant general records** for state militia are held at the Massachusetts Archives.
- Access: [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) (subscription) for NARA military records; NARA directly at [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/).

---

### 7. Naturalization Records

FamilySearch holds *Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906* (collection [1459213](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213)), which spans the full target period. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record (county, state, or federal), so also check Berkshire County Court of Common Pleas records.

---

### 8. Passenger Lists

FamilySearch holds *Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891* (collection [1784312](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312)), which aligns exactly with your target window. Relevant primarily if family members immigrated or if you are tracing origins.

---

### 9. Cemetery Records

[Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) indexes gravestones across Berkshire County, including pre-1850 markers, and is a useful cross-check for death dates and family groupings.

---

### 10. Historical Newspapers

# Finding Ancestor Marriage Records

Great question! Marriage records are among the most valuable genealogical sources. Here's how to approach the search:

---

## 🔍 Start With What You Know
Before searching, gather:
- **Full names** of both parties (including bride's maiden name if known)
- **Approximate marriage year** (estimate from children's birth years)
- **Location** — state, county, country

---

## 📂 Key Record Types to Search

| Record Type | What It Contains | Typical Date Range |
|---|---|---|
| **Marriage certificates** | Names, date, place, witnesses, officiants | 1800s–present |
| **Marriage bonds/licenses** | Groom's intent + surety | Colonial–1800s |
| **Marriage banns** | Public announcement (church) | 1600s–1900s |
| **Church registers** | Baptism, marriage, burial | 1500s–present |
| **Civil registration** | Government-recorded vital events | Varies by country |

---

## 🌐 Best Online Resources

- **[FamilySearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org)** — Free; largest collection of digitized marriage records worldwide
- **[Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com)** — Subscription; extensive U.S. and international collections
- **[FindMyPast](https://www.findmypast.com)** — Strong for UK, Ireland, and Australia
- **[Fold3](https://www.fold3.com)** — U.S. military and some county records
- **State/County vital records offices** — For certified copies

---

## 🏛️ Offline Sources
- **County courthouses** — Original marriage license books
- **Church archives** — Pre-civil registration records
- **State archives** — Statewide collections
- **Genealogical societies** — Often hold indexes for local records

---

## 💡 Tips for Hard-to-Find Marriages
1. **Search for witnesses** — often siblings or parents, which extends the family
2. **Check surrounding counties** — couples often married in the bride's home county
3. **Look at divorce records** — they often recite the original marriage date/place
4. **Search newspapers** — wedding announcements in local papers
5. **Try alternate spellings** of surnames

---

Would you like a more targeted guide? If you tell me the **location** (country, state, or county) and **time period** you're researching, I can give you a detailed locality guide for exactly what records exist and where to find them!

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 (FamilySearch place record dateRange `+1811/`; carved from Berks and Northampton Counties)
- **County seat:** Pottsville
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** `place_population` returned no data. County experienced rapid growth during the anthracite coal boom; 1850 Schuylkill County U.S. Federal Census confirmed on Ancestry.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominant throughout 1840–1880.
- **Ethnic composition:** Welsh, Irish, English, and German immigrants in mining communities (confirmed: German-language church records in FamilySearch vol. 007936751).
- **Religious denominations:** English and German denominations documented in vol. 007936751 (1842–1895).
- **Key historical events:** Civil War (1861–1865); Molly Maguires labor unrest and trials (1860s–1876).

## Boundary changes
- No historical jurisdiction changes returned by `place_search_all`. Boundaries stable from 1811.
- Pre-1811 records: Berks and Northampton Counties.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No statewide civil birth/death registration until 1906. County marriage registration confirmed from at least 1870 (earliest FamilySearch volume).
- **Marriage records:** Vol. 007936753 — Marriage Records, 1870–1910, 94 images, browse-only (0% indexed). Covers final decade of target window only.
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death records 1840–1880; no confirmed digitized marriage records before 1870.
- **Substitutes:** Church registers (vol. 007936751), census mortality schedules (1850–1880), cemetery records, newspaper notices.

### Church records
- **FamilySearch:** Vol. 007936751 — Church Records, 1842–1895, 187 images. Languages: English and German. Browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text). German entries require Kurrent paleography skill.
- **Other:** Local parish archives; Schuylkill County Historical Society; denominational archives.

### Census records
- **Federal:** 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880 decennial censuses. 1890 largely destroyed.
  - 1850 census confirmed indexed on Ancestry: https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/
  - Includes mortality schedules (1850–1880) — critical substitute for absent vital records.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct regular state censuses.

### Probate and court records
- **FamilySearch statewide:** Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (id: 1999196), 2,304,118 images — https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196
- **FamilySearch county volume:** Vol. 007936749 — Probate Records, 1851–1930, 412 images. Browse-only (0% indexed).
- **Held at:** Schuylkill County Courthouse (Register of Wills); Pennsylvania State Archives.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (state-land state; no federal GLO patents).
- **FamilySearch:** Vol. 007936752 — Deed Records, 1815–1900, 543 images, 22% name-indexed (partially searchable), not full-text.
- **Held at:** Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives (patents/warrants).
- **Pre-period tax lists on Ancestry:** Pennsylvania Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801 — https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/

### Military records
- **Conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); Civil War (1861–1865).
- **Records:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants, Civil War draft registrations (1863) at NARA. Pennsylvania adjutant general records at Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **No Schuylkill County-specific military volumes** returned by `volume_search`.

### Cemetery records
- No FindAGrave or BillionGraves links returned by `external_links_search`. Search these sites directly.
- Physical records at individual cemeteries and Schuylkill County Historical Society.

### Newspaper records
- No newspaper collections returned by tool results for this county and period.
- Check: Chronicling America (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/), Pennsylvania State Library, Schuylkill County Historical Society (*Miners' Journal*, Pottsville, est. 1825).

### Immigration/naturalization records
- **FamilySearch:** Vol. 007936750 — Naturalization Records, 1849–1915, 298 images. Browse-only (0% indexed). Covers 1849–1880 portion of target window.
- **Pre-1906:** Naturalizations could be filed in any court — search county vol. 007936750 AND NARA federal court records (Philadelphia).
- **Ports:** Philadelphia (primary); New York/Castle Garden.

### Tax records
- No in-period (1840–1880) tax records returned by tool results. Records exist physically at county/township level.
- Ancestry pre-period: Tax and Exoneration Lists, 1768–1801.

### Other record types
- **Coal mining:** Pennsylvania Dept. of Mines annual reports (State Library); company records (Historical Society of Pennsylvania).
- **Court records (civil/criminal):** Schuylkill County Courthouse; Molly Maguires trials (1875–1876) at courthouse.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collection | Date range | Access level | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, Probate Records (id: 1999196) | 1683–1994 | Images (2,304,118) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Vol. 007936752: Deed Records | 1815–1900 | 22% name-indexed; 78% browse-only | Free |
| FamilySearch | Vol. 007936750: Naturalization Records | 1849–1915 | Browse-only (0% indexed) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Vol. 007936749: Probate Records | 1851–1930 | Browse-only (0% indexed) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Vol. 007936751: Church Records (English/German) | 1842–1895 | Browse-only (0% indexed) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Vol. 007936753: Marriage Records | 1870–1910 | Browse-only (0% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry | 1850 U.S. Federal Census — Schuylkill County | 1850 | Indexed + images | Subscription |
| Ancestry | Pennsylvania Tax and Exoneration Lists (pre-period) | 1768–1801 | Indexed | Subscription |

**Coverage:** `volume_search` returned `totalResults: 5` with no `nextPageToken` — the above is the complete set. `external_links_search` returned `totalForPlace: 2`; both listed.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill County Courthouse, Pottsville, PA | Deeds, court records, naturalizations, probate, marriage licenses | In-person / mail |
| Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg, PA | State-land patents, military records, state collections | In-person; phmc.pa.gov |
| Schuylkill County Historical Society, Pottsville, PA | Cemetery surveys, local newspapers, genealogical files | In-person |
| NARA Philadelphia | Federal census, military service/pension, passenger lists, federal naturalizations | In-person / mail / Ancestry / Fold3 |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia | Coal company records, manuscript collections | In-person |
| Denominational archives | Church registers not yet digitized | Contact denomination |

## Records NOT online
- Civil birth and death records (do not exist for 1840–1880)
- Marriage records before 1870
- In-period tax/assessment records (1840–1880)
- Newspapers
- Coal company employment rolls and accident reports
- Molly Maguires and other criminal court files
- School records
- Fraternal and mutual aid society records

## Known record losses
FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania and Schuylkill County returned only a generic redirect — no county-specific loss information confirmed. Contact Schuylkill County Historical Society and courthouse to inquire.

## Research tips
1. No civil birth/death records 1840–1880 — use church registers (vol. 007936751), census mortality schedules (1850–1880), cemetery records, and newspapers.
2. Four of five FamilySearch volumes are browse-only (0% indexed) — plan for image-by-image browsing.
3. Deed records vol. 007936752: run name search first (22% indexed), then browse remaining ~78%.
4. German-language church records require Kurrent paleography skill.
5. Pre-1906 naturalizations: search both county vol. 007936750 and NARA federal court records.
6. 1850 census indexed on Ancestry: https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/
7. Coal mining records: Pennsylvania Dept. of Mines annual reports at State Library; company records at Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
8. Molly Maguires trials (1875–1876): extensive court records at Schuylkill County Courthouse; national newspaper coverage.
9. Adjoining counties (Berks, Carbon, Luzerne, Columbia, Northumberland, Dauphin): check for families near borders.
10. FamilySearch Wiki gap: consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Genealogy directly for additional guidance.

# 📍 Locality Research Guide
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania — 1840s–1860s

---

### Jurisdictional Context

**Schuylkill County** (`standardPlace`: *Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States*) was formed in **1811** from Berks and Northampton Counties. By the 1840s it was fully established with no boundary changes during the target period — all records from this era were created and filed under Schuylkill County.

**County seat:** Pottsville (established 1816), where court, deed, probate, and naturalization records were held.

**Context for this era:** Schuylkill County was the epicenter of Pennsylvania's **anthracite coal industry**. The 1840s–1860s brought massive waves of Welsh, Irish, English, and German immigrant miners. This immigration surge makes naturalization records, church records, and mining company records especially important alongside the standard genealogical sources.

> ⚠️ **Vital registration gap:** Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil registration** of births and deaths during the 1840s–1860s (statewide registration did not begin until 1906). Church records are the **primary substitute** for birth and death documentation in this period. Marriage licenses were issued at the county level and do survive.

---

### 📊 Population Context

`place_population` returned no data for Schuylkill County — no figures can be cited from tool output. For historical context, consult the decennial census schedules themselves (1840, 1850, 1860).

---

### Record-by-Record Survey

#### 1. 🗳️ Federal Census Records
**Access: Indexed + images (excellent)**

FamilySearch holds **1 digitized volume** covering Schuylkill County census records for the target period:

| Volume | IGN | Images | Indexed | Full-Text |
|--------|-----|--------|---------|-----------|
| U.S. Federal Census, 1850–1860 | 007621224 | 412 | **96%** | ✅ Yes |

- The 1850 Schuylkill County census is also available via Ancestry.com (confirmed external link).
- The **1840 census** (pre-slavery, pre-names-for-free-persons era) and **1870 census** were not returned as separate volumes in the search — check FamilySearch and Ancestry directly.
- **Mortality schedules** (listing deaths in the year preceding the census) were taken in 1850 and 1860; these were not returned in the volume search and may be browse-only or held separately at NARA or the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- The **1850 census was the first to name every household member** — a landmark for Schuylkill County given the large immigrant mining population.

**Repository:** FamilySearch.org (free); Ancestry.com (subscription)

---

#### 2. ⛪ Church Records
**Access: Browse-only images; partial German — must browse image-by-image with no name search**

FamilySearch holds **1 digitized volume** of Schuylkill County church records:

| Volume | IGN | Images | Indexed | Full-Text | Languages |
|--------|-----|--------|---------|-----------|-----------|
| Church Records (Lutheran), 1840–1875 | 004288771 | 198 | **0%** | ❌ No | English & **German** |

⚠️ **This volume has zero name-indexing and is not full-text searchable — it must be browsed page by page.** A portion of the content is in **German** (standard for German Lutheran parishes of the era); researchers must be able to read period German church record conventions.

Given the county's immigrant composition, the following denominations generated significant records during this period:
- **Lutheran** (German immigrants) — see volume above
- **German Reformed** — likely separate records, not found in volume search
- **Welsh Calvinist Methodist / Congregational** (Welsh miners)
- **Roman Catholic** (Irish and German miners)
- **Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal**

Church records not returned in the digitized volume search are likely **physical-only** at individual congregations, denominational archives, or on microfilm at FamilySearch. The **Presbyterian Historical Society** (Philadelphia) and **Catholic Diocese of Allentown** archives are key repositories for their respective denominations.

> 📋 **Note:** One collections_search result — *Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records* — was labeled in the tool output as a "synthetic test fixture" and has been excluded from this guide as it does not represent a verified FamilySearch collection.

---

#### 3. 📜 Probate Records
**Access: Full-text searchable but only 4% name-indexed — primarily browse or full-text**

Two FamilySearch resources cover Schuylkill County probate:

| Resource | ID / IGN | Images/Records | Indexed | Full-Text |
|----------|----------|---------------|---------|-----------|
| Schuylkill Co. Probate Records, 1845–1880 (volume) | 004812990 | 286 images | **4%** | ✅ Yes |
| Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (statewide collection) | 1999196 | 2,304,118 images | 0% (images only) | — |

The volume IGN 004812990 covers the target period well (1845–1880) and is full-text searchable, making it findable via keyword search even without name indexing. The statewide collection is image-only and browse-only.

Probate records include **wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, and guardianship files** — valuable for identifying heirs, property, and family relationships.

**Repository:** FamilySearch.org; physical originals at Schuylkill County Register of Wills, Pottsville.

---

#### 4. 🏠 Land & Deed Records
**Access: Likely physical-only or microfilm — not returned in digitized volume search**

No digitized FamilySearch volumes for Schuylkill County deed or land records were returned for 1840–1870. These records almost certainly exist in physical form:

- **Deed books** are held at the **Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds**, Pottsville.
- Pennsylvania is an **original land state** (not a federal land state), so land patents/warrants were issued by the Commonwealth, not the Bureau of Land Management. Early patents are at the **Pennsylvania State Archives**.
- **Tax lists** — the Ancestry.com collection of *Pennsylvania Tax and Exoneration Lists* covers only 1768–1801 (before the target period). Tax records from the 1840s–1860s were not returned in the digital survey and should be sought at the county courthouse or Pennsylvania State Archives.

---

#### 5. ⚖️ Court & Naturalization Records
**Access: Likely physical-only — not returned in digitized volume search**

No digitized FamilySearch volumes of Schuylkill County court or naturalization records were returned. However, these are among the **most important record types** given the massive immigration of miners in this era:

- **Naturalization records** (pre-1906) were filed in any Pennsylvania court of record — the Court of Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, or Orphans' Court. Physical volumes are at the **Schuylkill County Courthouse** and some are on microfilm at FamilySearch.
- **Court of Common Pleas** records include civil suits, equity cases, and name changes.
- **Quarter Sessions** records document criminal cases and minor civil matters.
- The **Orphans' Court** handled guardianship and estate matters for minors.

---

#### 6. ⚔️ Military Records
**Access: National Archives (NARA); some Pennsylvania state-level records**

The 1840s–1860s encompasses the **Mexican-American War (1846–1848)** and especially the **Civil War (1861–1865)**. Key records:

- **Civil War service records and pension files** — at NARA, Philadelphia (Mid-Atlantic Region) and Washington, D.C. Searchable on Fold3 (subscription) and via NARA's online catalog.
- **Civil War draft registrations (1863)** — the Consolidated Lists of Civil War Draft Registrations for Pennsylvania are on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Pennsylvania Civil War veterans' card file** — at the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- Schuylkill County contributed heavily to the Union cause; the county's mining population was heavily recruited into Pennsylvania volunteer infantry and cavalry regiments.

---

#### 7. 📰 Newspapers
**Access: Physical and digitized — check multiple repositories**

The **Miners' Journal** (Pottsville, est. 1825) was the dominant newspaper of the anthracite region throughout this period. It published birth, marriage, and death notices, legal notices, and extensive coverage of the coal industry and immigrant community. It is an exceptional source for this era.

- Digitized issues may be available through **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress, free) and **GenealogyBank** (subscription).
- Physical collections at the **Historical Society of Schuylkill County**, Pottsville.

---

#### 8. 🏛️ Local Repository: Historical Society of Schuylkill County
The **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville) holds local collections not found in any online survey — cemetery records, family files, Bible records, church histories, and county histories. This is a high-priority repository for any Schuylkill County research.

---

### 🌐 Online Resources

| Platform | Resource | Notes |
|----------|----------|-------|
| FamilySearch.org | Census volume 007621224 | 1850–1860, 96% indexed, free |
| FamilySearch.org | Probate volume 004812990 | 1845–1880, full-text searchable |
| FamilySearch.org | Lutheran church volume 004288771 | 1840–1875, browse-only, partial German |
| FamilySearch.org | PA Probate Records 1683–1994 | Statewide, image-only |
| Ancestry.com | 1850 U.S. Federal Census – Schuylkill County | Confirmed curated link |
| Fold3 | Civil War service records & pensions | Subscription |
| Chronicling America | Miners' Journal issues | Free; check coverage dates |

---

### ⚠️ Key Quirks & Research Warnings

1. **No Pennsylvania statewide vital registration in this period.** Births and deaths were recorded only by churches. Marriage licenses were issued at the county level (Schuylkill County Courthouse).
2. **Lutheran church records are browse-only and partially in German.** Researchers must page through image-by-image and read period German church Latin/German entries.
3. **Probate volume is only 4% name-indexed** — use full-text search rather than name search.
4. **Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any Schuylkill County court** — check Common Pleas, Quarter Sessions, and Orphans' Court separately.

# Locality Research Guide: Alabama Region, c. 1780–1819 (Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdictional Overview

At 1800, the area we now call Alabama did **not yet exist as a state** — it became a state only in December 1819. Records created around 1800 will be filed under a layered set of predecessor jurisdictions, not under "Alabama." Understanding which authority governed your ancestor's location is essential before searching.

| Period | Governing Jurisdiction | Notes |
|--------|----------------------|-------|
| Pre-1763 | French colony (Louisiana/Mobile) | Mobile founded 1702 |
| 1763–1780 | British West Florida | British colonial reorganization |
| 1780–1813 | Spanish West Florida (Mobile District) | Spain recaptured Mobile 1780; retained it until 1813 |
| 1798–1817 | **Mississippi Territory** (U.S.) | Organized 1798; encompassed all of present-day Mississippi and Alabama |
| 1817–1819 | **Alabama Territory** (U.S.) | Split from Mississippi Territory 1817; statehood December 14, 1819 |

> **Critical county-formation quirk:** Around 1800, **Washington County** (organized 1800) covered most of present-day Alabama north of Mobile. Counties carved from it include Madison (1808), Baldwin (1809), and Mobile (1812). You must identify which county held authority over your ancestor's location and search accordingly — the county is the filing unit for most court, probate, and land records.

> **Southern Alabama quirk:** The Mobile area remained **Spanish territory until 1813**, meaning an ancestor in the Mobile District c. 1800 was under Spanish governance, not U.S. territorial authority. Spanish civil and ecclesiastical records apply there, not Mississippi Territory records.

---

## Record Types, Repositories & Digitization

### 1. Territorial Census Substitutes (1801–1816)
The Mississippi Territory conducted census enumerations in **1801, 1805, 1808, 1810, and 1816** that covered the Alabama portion of the territory. These are among the most important substitutes for the destroyed 1800 and 1810 federal censuses for this region.

- **Repositories:** Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery; Mississippi Department of Archives and History (MDAH), Jackson
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890* (collection ID 2016756) — **287,634 indexed records, index only, no images** ([familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756)). This covers 1810 onward; the 1801 and 1805 enumerations are likely **physical/microfilm only** at ADAH and MDAH.
- **Access:** For 1801 and 1805, contact ADAH directly or consult their microfilm holdings.
- *(Source: wiki_search result, "Mississippi Territory Genealogy," [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Territory_Genealogy#Territorial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Territory_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))*

---

### 2. Federal Land Records (1803+)
Federal land sales in the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory began in **1803** through two land offices:
- **St. Stephens Land Office** — served south Alabama (Washington County area)
- **Huntsville Land Office** — served north Alabama (Madison County area)

Entry files (applications, warrants, certificates) are in **National Archives Record Group 49**. Many patents are digitized and searchable at **BLM General Land Office Records** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)), which is a free, indexed online resource.

- **Repositories:** NARA (Atlanta regional facility covers Alabama); BLM GLO online
- **Digitization:** BLM GLO patents — **indexed + images** (name-searchable online). NARA entry files — physical, must be requested or visited.
- *(Source: wiki_search result, "Mississippi Territory Genealogy," [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Territory_Genealogy#Territorial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Territory_Genealogy#Territorial_Records))*

---

### 3. Territorial Court, Tax & Militia Records (1798–1819)
The Mississippi Territory government created court files, tax lists, and militia rolls covering what is now Alabama. These are among the richest name-dense records for the period.

- **Repository:** ADAH (Montgomery) holds the largest Alabama-focused collection; MDAH (Jackson) holds records for the Mississippi portion that may name Alabama families.
- **Digitization:** Largely **physical or microfilm only** — not yet reflected in FamilySearch's Alabama collections (which begin at 1809 at the earliest). Check ADAH's online catalog at [archives.alabama.gov](https://archives.alabama.gov).

---

### 4. Spanish Colonial Records — Mobile District (1780–1813)
For ancestors in the Mobile area, the governing authority c. 1800 was **Spain**. Spanish colonial records include census returns (*padrones*), church registers, and land grants (*mercedes*).

- **Primary archive:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain — holds original Spanish administrative records for the Mobile District
- **Copies:** Library of Congress, Washington, DC — holds transcripts and microfilm of Spanish colonial records
- **Local access:** Mobile Municipal Archives, Mobile, AL — holds French and Spanish colonial microfilm
- **Digitization:** Largely **physical and microfilm only**; some transcriptions published in printed finding aids. Not in FamilySearch's Alabama digital collections.
- *(Source: wiki_search result, "Alabama Genealogy," [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))*

---

### 5. Church Records (1803+)
No civil vital registration existed in this period — **Alabama did not require statewide vital registration until 1908**. Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are therefore the primary source for vital events c. 1800.

- **Active denominations c. 1800:** Methodist, Baptist, and Presbyterian congregations established early in the territory; Catholic parishes in the Mobile area (continuing from French and Spanish periods)
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950* (collection ID 1986396) — **156,789 indexed records, 78,394 images** ([familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396)). Starts 1803; sparse for the earliest years.
- **Digitization:** **Indexed + images** for records in this collection. Pre-1803 and undigitized records require checking denominational archives and ADAH.

---

### 6. Marriage Records (1809+)
County-level marriage bonds and licenses began once counties were formally organized.

- **FamilySearch collection:** *Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950* (collection ID 1598408) — **612,345 indexed records, 306,172 images** ([familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408))
- **Digitization:** **Indexed + images**
- **Note:** For marriages before 1809, church records and any surviving territorial court registers are your only recourse. Washington County records from 1800 are the earliest county-level records for most of Alabama.

---

### 7. Probate Records (1809+)
Wills, estate inventories, and letters of administration were filed at the county level from county formation onward.

- **FamilySearch collection:** *Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985* (collection ID 1537764) — **438,210 indexed records, 219,105 images** ([familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764))
- **Digitization:** **Indexed + images**
- **Note:** Pre-1809 probate from Washington County would be in territorial court records at ADAH.

---

### 8. Military Records
- **War of 1812 (1812–1815):** Many Alabama Territory residents served; service records and pension files are at NARA and partially digitized on **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)).
- **Mississippi Territory militia rolls (c. 1800):** At ADAH; primarily physical.
- **Creek War / early frontier engagements:** Check NARA pension files (bounty land warrants and pension applications often document family relationships and ages).

---

### 9. French Colonial Records (pre-1763)
Not directly applicable to c. 1800, but useful for tracing Mobile-area families back further.
- **Repository:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives
- *(Source: wiki_search result, "Alabama Genealogy," [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))*

---

### 10. Newspapers
Early newspapers circulated in Mobile and Natchez. Holdings are patchy for c. 1800.
- **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com)) — limited for this early period
- ADAH holds early Alabama newspaper microfilm

---

### 11. Cemetery Records
- **FindAGrave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) — indexes many Alabama cemeteries, though coverage for unmarked or early frontier graves is thin
- ADAH also has some compiled cemetery transcription collections

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Location | What it Holds |
|-----------|----------|---------------|
| **Alabama Dept of Archives & History (ADAH)** | Montgomery, AL | Territorial censuses, militia, court, land, tax records; microfilm; state archives — [archives.alabama.gov](https://archives.alabama.gov) |
| **Mississippi Dept of Archives & History (MDAH)** | Jackson, MS | Mississippi Territory records (co-holder); [mdah.ms.gov](https://www.mdah.ms.gov) |
| **National Archives — Atlanta** | Atlanta, GA | Federal land records (RG 49), military records, federal court files |
| **BLM General Land Office** | Online | Federal land patents, 1803+ — [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) |
| **Archivo General de Indias** | Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial records for Mobile District |
| **Library of Congress** | Washington, DC | Transcripts/copies of Spanish colonial records |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives** | Mobile, AL | French and Spanish colonial microfilm |
| **FamilySearch** | Online | 4 Alabama collections (1803–1950); see collection IDs above |

---

## Digitization Summary

| Record Type | Earliest Date | FamilySearch Status | Best Online Access |
|-------------|---------------|--------------------|--------------------|
| Territorial censuses (1801, 1805) | 1801 | **Physical/microfilm only** (ADAH, MDAH) | None yet |
| Census substitutes index (1810+) | 1810 | **Indexed, no images** | FamilySearch col. 2016756 |
| Federal land patents | 1803 | **Indexed + images** | BLM GLO |
| NARA land entry files | 1803 | **Physical** | NARA Atlanta |
| Church records | 1803 | **Indexed + images** (partial) | FamilySearch col. 1986396 |
| County marriages | 1809 | **Indexed + images** | FamilySearch col. 1598408 |
| Probate records | 1809 | **Indexed + images** | FamilySearch col. 1537764 |
| Spanish colonial records | pre-1813 | **Physical/microfilm** (Seville, LOC) | None digitized |
| Territorial court/tax/militia | 1798 | **Physical/microfilm** (ADAH, MDAH) | None yet |

---

## Key Research Quirks & Cautions

1. **Alabama didn't exist as a jurisdiction c. 1800** — search under *Mississippi Territory*, not "Alabama," for territorial-era records at NARA, MDAH, and most finding aids.
2. **County boundary changes are essential.** Washington County (1800) covered most of the state at first. Identify which county held authority when your event occurred before searching courthouse or probate records.
3. **South Alabama (Mobile area) was Spanish territory until 1813.** An ancestor there c. 1800 appears in Spanish colonial records — not U.S. territorial records. Search the Archivo General de Indias and Library of Congress transcripts, or Mobile Municipal Archives microfilm.
4. **No statewide civil vital registration until 1908.** Church records, county marriage bonds, and territorial court documents are your only sources for births, marriages, and deaths before that.
5. **FamilySearch's Alabama collections begin at 1803–1809** — coverage of the period right around 1800 is thin in digitized/indexed form. Physical research at ADAH is necessary for pre-1803 and for the earliest territorial censuses.
6. **The 1810 federal census is the first U.S. census to cover present-day Alabama** — earlier censuses did not extend to this territory. Territorial enumerations (1801, 1805, 1808) substitute for the 1800 federal census.
7. **BLM GLO is a free, searchable resource** for federal land patents starting 1803 — an often-overlooked first step for locating an ancestor on the landscape.

# Locality Research Guide: Arkansas Region, Pre-1800 (Spanish Colonial Period)

## Jurisdictional History

The Arkansas region before 1800 passed through two European colonial hands, creating a **temporal split** that governs which language, which archive, and which record series applies:

| Period | Controlling Power | Administrative Unit |
|---|---|---|
| 1686–1763 | France | French Louisiana (Province of Louisiana) |
| 1763–1800 | Spain | Spanish Louisiana (Luisiana) |
| 1800 onward | France → United States | Louisiana Territory / Arkansas Territory (1819) |

**Arkansas Post** (established 1686) was the sole significant European settlement in the region throughout this entire period. Virtually every pre-1800 genealogical record for the Arkansas region originates from this one military-civil post, located in what is now Arkansas County. County-level civil infrastructure did not exist before 1800; Arkansas County itself was not organized until 1813.

> **Quirk — two-era research trail:** For ancestors at Arkansas Post, you may need to work both the French-era record set (pre-1763, in French) and the Spanish-era set (1763–1800, in Spanish). Although they cover the same physical place, they are held in different repositories and written in different languages. Treat them as a single continuous research trail — don't stop at 1763 in either direction.

---

## Records Available and Their Access Levels

### 1. Sacramental Registers (Church Records)
**Spanish period: 1763–1800 | French period: early 1700s–1763**

Catholic missionaries maintained baptism, marriage, and burial registers at Arkansas Post throughout both periods. These are the **primary genealogical source** for this era — they name European settlers, mixed-heritage families, enslaved individuals, and sometimes Native Americans.

- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Image Group **008814402** — *Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial), Arkansas Post, Arkansas County, 1763–1800.* 64 images. **Browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Records are **in Spanish**; you must read the originals. Access via FamilySearch by browsing the image group directly.
- **Physical/transcriptions:** The Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock holds original or transcribed registers. The Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock) holds transcriptions. ([FamilySearch Wiki – Arkansas Genealogy, Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records))
- **French-era registers** (pre-1763): Written in French. Some are held by the Diocese of Little Rock and the Arkansas History Commission; additional copies may be at the Archives nationales d'outre-mer (Aix-en-Provence, France).

**Access level: One browse-only digitized Spanish-era volume on FamilySearch; remainder physical or microfilm only.**

---

### 2. Colonial Censuses (Padrones)
**Spanish period: 1769–1800**

The Spanish colonial administration conducted periodic household censuses (padrones) at Arkansas Post listing heads of household, family members, ages, and sometimes racial designations. These are among the most useful genealogical substitutes for civil vital registration, which did not exist.

- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock), Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain), and on microfilm at the Library of Congress. ([FamilySearch Wiki – Arkansas Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **FamilySearch coverage:** No indexed collection found for pre-1800 Arkansas padrones. Not covered by the three FamilySearch Arkansas collections (all date 1819 or later).
- **Language:** Spanish.

**Access level: Physical/microfilm only; not digitized or indexed on FamilySearch.**

---

### 3. Land Records (Concessions and Grants)
**Spanish period: 1769–1800 | French period: 1686–1763**

Spanish (and earlier French) colonial officials issued land concessions at Arkansas Post. These record the grantee's name, land description, and sometimes family circumstances.

- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias (Seville); NARA holds some Spanish land grant records confirmed under subsequent U.S. territorial law. ([FamilySearch Wiki – Arkansas Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))
- **Online access:** The Archivo General de Indias has partially digitized its holdings at [PARES (Portal de Archivos Españoles)](http://pares.mcu.es) — searchable online, free, but records are in Spanish and require paleographic skill.
- **FamilySearch coverage:** No pre-1800 land record collection found for Arkansas.

**Access level: Physical and partially online (PARES); not on FamilySearch.**

---

### 4. Military Post Records
**Spanish period: 1763–1800**

Arkansas Post maintained a Spanish garrison. Military records include muster rolls, officer correspondence, and administrative reports that may name soldiers and their families.

- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias (Seville); microfilm copies at the Library of Congress.
- **FamilySearch coverage:** None found for pre-1800 Arkansas military records.
- **Language:** Spanish.

**Access level: Physical and microfilm only; not on FamilySearch.**

---

### 5. Civil and Notarial Records
**Spanish period: 1769–1800**

Civil registers from the post's administration may include contracts, wills, and other notarial acts recorded by the post commandant or appointed notary.

- **Where held:** Arkansas History Commission; Archivo General de Indias.
- **FamilySearch coverage:** None found.

**Access level: Physical only; not on FamilySearch.**

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock, AR) | Transcriptions of colonial records, padrones, church register copies, land records | In-person and some online finding aids; [https://www.archives.arkansas.gov](https://www.archives.arkansas.gov) |
| **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain) | Spanish colonial administrative records, military records, land concessions | Partially digitized at [http://pares.mcu.es](http://pares.mcu.es); records in Spanish |
| **Library of Congress** (Washington, DC) | Microfilm of colonial records from Arkansas Post period | In-person microfilm reading room |
| **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** | Original/transcribed sacramental registers | Contact diocese archivist |
| **FamilySearch** | 1 browse-only digitized volume of Spanish colonial sacramental registers (image group 008814402) | Free at FamilySearch.org |
| **NARA** (Washington, DC) | Some Spanish land grant confirmations under U.S. territorial law | In-person or [https://www.archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov) |
| **Archives nationales d'outre-mer** (Aix-en-Provence, France) | French colonial records pre-1763 | In-person; some digital finding aids online |

---

## FamilySearch Collections (Post-1800 Context)

The three indexed FamilySearch collections for Arkansas all postdate 1800 and are **not** primary sources for the Spanish colonial period, but they may be useful as **bridge sources** if an ancestor appears in early Arkansas records shortly after the Louisiana Purchase:

| Collection | Date Range | Records |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819–1870 | 1819–1870 | 178,345 indexed records |
| Arkansas, County Marriages, 1837–1957 | 1837–1957 | 389,210 indexed records |
| Arkansas, Freedmen's Bureau Field Office Records, 1865–1872 | 1865–1872 | 45,678 indexed records |

---

## Key Research Quirks and Cautions

1. **All records are at Arkansas Post** — the region had no other European settlement before 1800. If your ancestor was in what is now Arkansas, they were almost certainly connected to Arkansas Post or transient through it.
2. **No civil vital registration existed** — birth, marriage, and death records survive only in Catholic sacramental registers. If the church register has a gap, there is likely no substitute.
3. **Language barrier is significant** — Spanish-era records (1763–1800) are in Spanish; French-era records (pre-1763) are in French. Both may use archaic paleographic scripts. Engage a translator familiar with colonial ecclesiastical Latin and period Spanish or French handwriting.
4. **The single FamilySearch volume (008814402) must be browsed image-by-image** — there is no name index or full-text search. Plan to examine all 64 images.
5. **Spanish land grants were confirmed under U.S. law** — if an ancestor held land at Arkansas Post, a record of that claim may appear in U.S. territorial-era land records (post-1803) even though the original grant was Spanish. Search NARA and BLM General Land Office records as a downstream trail.
6. **Records before 1763 were created under French jurisdiction** — search both the French-era and Spanish-era series rather than treating 1763 as a hard boundary. Families often appear in both.
7. **PARES (Archivo General de Indias online portal)** is the most underused resource for this period — free, substantial, and directly relevant. Requires comfort with 18th-century Spanish documentary script.

---

## Recommended Research Sequence

1. Browse FamilySearch image group **008814402** (Spanish colonial sacramental registers, 1763–1800) in full.
2. Contact the **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** archivist for any registers not on FamilySearch and for the French-period registers.
3. Search the **Arkansas History Commission** for padrones and transcribed colonial records.
4. Search **PARES** ([http://pares.mcu.es](http://pares.mcu.es)) using the ancestor's name and "Luisiana" or "Arkansas" as search terms.
5. Check the **Library of Congress** microfilm holdings for Arkansas Post records.
6. If the family appears in U.S. records soon after 1803, trace their land claims through NARA and BLM GLO to find the underlying Spanish concession.

# 🗺️ Locality Guide: Ohio / Northwest Territory, c. 1790 (pre-statehood)

---

## Jurisdictional Context

**The single most important thing to know**: in 1790, **Ohio did not exist**. What is now Ohio was part of the **Northwest Territory**, established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Ohio was the first state carved from that territory, admitted in **1803**. All records created before that date were generated under territorial authority, not Ohio state authority.

### County formation — the critical boundary puzzle

| County | Formed | Area covered |
|--------|--------|-------------|
| **Washington County** | 1788 | All of the Northwest Territory east of the Scioto River initially; the territorial capital was at Marietta |
| **Hamilton County** | 1790 | Southwestern Ohio (Cincinnati area) |

In 1790, **your ancestor lived in one of exactly these two counties** (or on land not yet organized into a county). You must determine which before you can know where records were filed. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Ohio Genealogy — Northwest Territory](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory)), "boundary changes were frequent — researchers must determine which county held jurisdiction at the time of the event."

### Three distinct land districts — each with its own records

Ohio has three land systems that create a **geographic split** affecting where records are held:

| District | Location | Survey System | Primary Record Repository |
|----------|----------|---------------|--------------------------|
| **Virginia Military District** | Between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers | Metes-and-bounds | Virginia State Library (warrants); local county (deeds) |
| **Connecticut Western Reserve** | Northeastern Ohio | Township/range (Connecticut grid) | Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland |
| **U.S. Public Land Survey** | Most of the rest of Ohio | Federal township/range | BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov); county deed books |

⚠️ **Which district holds your ancestor's land records depends entirely on where within Ohio they lived.** These are not a temporal split (before/after a date) but a **geographic split** — you cannot assume one repository without knowing the ancestor's location. Search all three if the location is unknown.

---

## Available Records & Access Levels

### 🔴 Vital Records (Births, Deaths)
**Gap: No civil registration existed in 1790 Ohio.** Ohio did not have statewide vital registration until the twentieth century. County-level death registration began in 1867; birth registration in 1867 (though compliance was poor for decades). For 1790, **church records are your only vital substitute**.

---

### ⛪ Church Records
**FamilySearch collection**: [Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917) — 678,234 records across 339,117 images, dating from **1787**.
- **Access level**: Indexed + images (searchable by name)
- Early frontier Ohio was served primarily by **Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist** circuit riders; Catholic missionaries were also present
- Coverage is uneven for the 1787–1803 window — many frontier communities had no established congregation
- Also check denominational archives directly (e.g., Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia)

---

### 💍 Marriage Records
**FamilySearch collection**: [Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785) — 1,523,678 records (3,047,356 persons) across 761,839 images, dating from **1789**.
- **Access level**: Indexed + images
- Earliest entries are from **Washington County** (1789) — the first organized county
- Hamilton County records begin 1790
- Marriage licenses were issued by county courts; the territorial court at Marietta (Washington County) held earliest jurisdiction

---

### 🏠 Land Records
Land records are the **single most productive source** for 1790 Ohio research, because land transactions were carefully documented even when vital and census records did not exist.

**FamilySearch collection**: [Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187) — 234,567 records across 117,283 images.
- **Access level**: Indexed + images

**FamilySearch digitized volume**: Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records, **1788–1799** (imageGroupNumber: 005112233) — 51 images
- **Access level**: ⚠️ Browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be viewed image-by-image with no search capability.
- Coverage: Northwest Territory broadly; these are the earliest territorial-era land records on FamilySearch

**BLM General Land Office** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov/)): Federal land patents for Ohio public lands — searchable online for free. Essential for the U.S. Public Land Survey District.

**Virginia Military District**: Warrants at the **Virginia State Library**, Richmond; county deed books in the relevant Ohio county for later conveyances.

**Connecticut Western Reserve**: Primary records at the **Western Reserve Historical Society**, Cleveland.

---

### 💰 Tax Records
**FamilySearch collection**: [Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542) — 345,890 records across 172,945 images.
- **Access level**: Indexed + images
- Begins **1800** — just after the 1790 target year, but useful for tracing continuity of residence

**FamilySearch digitized volume**: Washington County Tax Records, **1799–1803** (imageGroupNumber: 005112240) — 73 images
- **Access level**: ⚠️ Partially searchable — 12% name-indexed; not full-text searchable. Most images require browsing.
- This is the closest surviving tax volume to 1790; no earlier tax volumes were returned in the survey (2 total volumes found)

---

### 📜 Census Records
- The **1790 federal census** technically covered the Northwest Territory, but **enumeration of the Ohio territory was fragmentary and survival is limited**. Do not expect to find your ancestor in the 1790 census.
- The **1800 federal census** is the first to include the Ohio territory comprehensively, shortly before statehood.
- **No territorial or state census** for Ohio in the 1790 window was returned by the survey.

---

### ⚖️ Court & Probate Records
- Territorial courts operated out of **Marietta (Washington County)** and later Hamilton County
- Early court records (wills, estate inventories, guardianship, civil suits) are held at the **Ohio History Connection** (State Archives), 800 E. 17th Ave., Columbus, OH 43211 — per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Ohio Genealogy — Northwest Territory](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory))
- County courthouses hold later deed books and probate files once counties were established
- No court/probate volumes for this period appeared in the FamilySearch volume search, suggesting these records are **physical or microfilm only** at the Ohio History Connection

---

### 🎖️ Military Records
- Many early Ohio settlers were **Revolutionary War veterans** who received bounty land in the Virginia Military District
- Service records and **pension files** are at the **National Archives (NARA)**, Washington D.C.
- Pension files often contain rich biographical data (age, place of birth, family members)
- **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)) hosts many digitized Revolutionary War pension files
- Virginia Military District bounty land warrants are at the **Virginia State Library**

---

### 📰 Newspapers & Other Sources
- **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)) holds historical Ohio newspapers, though pre-1800 coverage is sparse
- **Find A Grave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/)) for cemetery inscriptions — early frontier grave markers occasionally survive and predate civil registration

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What it holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Marriages (1789+), Church Records (1787+), Land Records (1787+), Tax Records (1800+), 2 pre-statehood digitized volumes | Free online |
| **Ohio History Connection** (Columbus) | Territorial court/probate records, early land records | Physical / microfilm; some digitized |
| **Western Reserve Historical Society** (Cleveland) | Connecticut Western Reserve land records | Physical; some online via WRHS |
| **Virginia State Library** (Richmond, VA) | Virginia Military District warrants | Physical |
| **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents | Free online |
| **NARA** (Washington D.C.) | Revolutionary War service records, pension files | Physical; Fold3 for digitized pensions |
| **County courthouses** | Deed books, probate files (Washington Co. from 1788, Hamilton Co. from 1790) | Physical |

---

## Key Quirks & Researcher Warnings

1. **Search "Northwest Territory," not "Ohio,"** for pre-1803 records. FamilySearch's volume survey returned a volume explicitly labeled *Northwest Territory, United States* — this is the correct jurisdictional label for 1790 events.

2. **Washington County (1788) vs. Hamilton County (1790) split is geographic.** Which county holds your ancestor's records depends on exactly where they lived. An ancestor in the Cincinnati area is Hamilton County; one near Marietta is Washington County. If location is unknown, search both.

3. **The Virginia Military District records are in Virginia, not Ohio.** Land warrants for this zone are at the Virginia State Library, Richmond — not at the Ohio History Connection or any Ohio county courthouse.

4. **The Connecticut Western Reserve records are at a separate Cleveland repository.** Do not assume county courthouse or state archives for northeastern Ohio land records.

5. **Two pre-statehood digitized volumes on FamilySearch, both limited.** The Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records (1788–1799, 51 images) are **0% indexed** and must be browsed image-by-image. Washington County Tax Records (1799–1803, 73 images) are only 12% indexed.

6. **No civil vital registration existed in 1790.** Church records (FamilySearch collection 2246917, from 1787) are your only substitute for births, marriages, and deaths — and coverage is patchy on the frontier.

7. **The 1790 federal census gives minimal coverage for the Ohio territory.** The 1800 census is the first reliable enumeration. Don't rule out census research — just start at 1800 and work forward.
