# Locality Guide: California, United States — Gold Rush Era (1848–1865)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** California was admitted as the 31st U.S. state on **September 9, 1850**, bypassing territorial status entirely. From February 2, 1848 (Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo) to September 1850, it was an unorganized U.S. possession; before that, **Alta California** under Mexican and then Spanish rule.
- **Administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital from 1854); San Francisco was the principal commercial and arrival hub throughout the Gold Rush.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Before 1848 — Mexico (Alta California). 1848–1850 — U.S. military district (no formal civil government). 1850 onward — State of California.
- **Population during period:** California's population exploded from roughly 14,000 non-Native residents in 1848 to an estimated **92,597** enumerated in the 1850 federal census; approximately **300,000 migrants** arrived by 1855 (Wikipedia: *California Gold Rush*). No population data was returned by the `place_population` tool for this period.
- **Economy:** Placer and hard-rock gold mining dominated 1848–1855; commerce, shipping, agriculture, and ranching grew alongside it. Mining gradually industrialized through the late 1850s.
- **Ethnic composition:** Extraordinarily diverse — Yankee Americans, Californios (Mexican/Spanish Californians), Chilean and Peruvian miners, Chinese laborers (substantial from 1852), Irish, German, French, Australian, Hawaiian, and free and enslaved African Americans, among others.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (established from the Mission era), Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Episcopal, Jewish congregations in San Francisco; Protestant churches spread rapidly to mining towns.
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovery at Sutter's Mill (January 24, 1848); mass overland and sea migration ("Forty-Niners") 1849–1852; California Admission Day September 9, 1850; Foreign Miners' Tax (1850, 1852) targeting Chinese and Latin American miners; San Francisco fires of 1849–1851 (destroyed many early city records).

---

## Boundary changes

- **Pre-1848:** Records were generated under **Alta California / Mexican colonial administration** — entirely separate jurisdictional lineage. Mission records (Franciscan sacramental registers, 1769–1834) and some Mexican-era civil records predate U.S. jurisdiction.
- **1848–1850:** Unorganized U.S. possession under military governance; virtually no civil record infrastructure existed. Few records survive from this window.
- **1850 onward:** California created **27 original counties** at statehood; additional counties were carved out continuously through the 1850s–1860s. A miner's records may sit in a *different* county than the one that now covers that location — always identify the county that held jurisdiction in the *specific year* of interest.
- **Key mining counties formed 1850:** El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Amador, Sacramento, Mariposa, Shasta, Trinity, Yuba, and others. Boundaries shifted repeatedly; check the *California County Formation* history before routing searches.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Registration level and start:** California recorded births and marriages at the **county level** beginning at statehood (1850), per FamilySearch collection data. However, county-level registration in the 1850s was inconsistent and far from complete — Gold Rush mining camps were transient and poorly administered. **Statewide civil registration** did not become mandatory in California until the early twentieth century; the FamilySearch Wiki pages for California did not load through this tool (generic page returned), so a specific statewide date cannot be confirmed from tools — consult [FamilySearch Wiki: California Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy) directly for that detail.
- **What exists on FamilySearch:**
  - **California, County Births, 1850–1919** (Collection ID 2017276): 789,456 records, held at the county level. [Search here](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2017276)
  - **California, County Marriages, 1850–1952** (Collection ID 1452832): 567,890 records, county level. [Search here](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1452832)
- **Gap:** No FamilySearch death collection for this period appeared in the results — death registration in the 1850s was especially sparse. Mortality schedules in the 1850 and 1860 federal census (see below) are the primary substitute.
- **Pre-registration alternative:** Church records and newspaper notices (see below).

### Church records

- **Catholic (Mission era):** The **California, Mission Records, 1769–1850** collection (ID 1804372) on FamilySearch holds 98,765 records covering Franciscan sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) from 21 missions. These document Native Californian, Spanish colonial, and early Mexican-era individuals. [Access here](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1804372) — important background context for families with deep California roots, but outside the Gold Rush migration target window.
- **Protestant and Jewish:** Congregations formed rapidly in mining towns and San Francisco from 1849. Records remain scattered — held by individual parishes, diocesan archives, or the **California State Library**. Limited digitization.
- **Language note:** Mission-era records are in **Latin and Spanish** and require reading proficiency or a translation tool.

### Census records

- **1850 Federal Census (California):** The *first* federal census taken in California after statehood — critical for Gold Rush arrivals. **Partially destroyed** — some county returns are missing (per FamilySearch Wiki search result: *California Genealogy, Pre-Statehood Records*). Search what survives.
- **1852 California State Census:** A unique and essential record for this period — taken between federal censuses, it captures the peak Gold Rush population. FamilySearch volume **006601001** holds this census: 522 images, **88% name-indexed and full-text searchable** — the most accessible single source for 1850s California ancestors.
- **1860 Federal Census:** Complete for California; names all free residents with age, birthplace, and occupation — key for confirming where miners settled by the end of the decade. Includes mortality and agricultural schedules.
- **Mortality Schedules (1850, 1860):** List individuals who died in the 12 months preceding the census — valuable given the high mortality of the mining era.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration (for those who died intestate — no will — as many miners did), guardianship files, naturalizations, civil and criminal cases.
- **Held at:** **County Superior Courts** and county courthouses. For Gold Rush miners, probate filings in El Dorado, Placer, Tuolumne, and other mining counties may document personal property, tools, and sometimes name next-of-kin back in the home state.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 declarations of intention and petitions for naturalization were filed in *any* court of record — county, district, or federal. San Francisco held the largest volume of naturalization filings; many immigrants declared intention at arrival and filed petitions later in the interior counties.
- **Digitization:** No specific California probate or court volumes appeared in the `volume_search` first page results; these likely require in-person or mail access at county courthouses or the **California State Archives**.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** California is a **federal-land state** — the U.S. General Land Office (GLO/BLM) administered public land patents. Original land grants to settlers are searchable at the [BLM General Land Office Records website](https://glorecords.blm.gov/).
- **Mining claims:** A distinctive Gold Rush record type. **Mining Claim Registers** held at county recorders' offices documented placer and lode claims. FamilySearch volume **006601002** covers San Francisco mining claim registers 1849–1855: 340 images, **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only** image by image. Original registers for other mining counties (El Dorado, Placer, Tuolumne, etc.) are held at county recorders' offices, largely not digitized.
- **Mexican/Spanish land grants:** Rancho grants under Mexican law were adjudicated by the U.S. Land Commission after 1851 — records held at the **National Archives, Pacific Region (San Bruno)** and the **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley**.
- **Deeds:** County recorder's offices; limited digitization for the 1850s.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848) immediately preceded the Gold Rush; many veterans became '49ers. The Civil War (1861–1865) generated California volunteer unit records.
- **Mexican-American War:** Service records and pension files at **NARA** (Washington, D.C.); bounty land warrants at the **BLM GLO** site.
- **California Civil War Volunteers:** Service records at NARA and the **California State Archives**. The 1890 Veterans' Census schedule (mostly destroyed nationally) named Civil War veterans — check surviving schedules.
- **Access:** Fold3.com holds digitized NARA service records and pension files (subscription).

### Cemetery records

- **Coverage:** Major cemeteries of the era include Laurel Hill (San Francisco, since removed), Sacramento City Cemetery, and numerous miners' cemeteries in the foothills — many informal and poorly documented.
- **Online:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) holds transcriptions for many California cemeteries; coverage of remote mining-camp burials is sparse.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers, where they survive, are held by county agencies or historical societies.

### Newspaper records

- **Key papers:** *Alta California* (San Francisco, 1849–1891) is the premier Gold Rush–era newspaper — obituaries, shipping arrivals, mining news, and legal notices. *Sacramento Union* (1851–). Dozens of short-lived mining-camp papers also existed.
- **Where held:** [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com) and [Chronicling America](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) (Library of Congress, free) hold digitized California newspapers; the **California Digital Newspaper Collection** (CDNC) at UC Riverside offers free access to *Alta California* and others.
- **Value:** Arrival and departure notices, business partnerships, mining accidents, inquests, estate sales, and naturalization notices all appear in Gold Rush–era papers.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Overland migrants:** No formal federal arrival records exist for the overland trails (California, Oregon, Santa Fe). Trail diaries, journals, and emigrant lists compiled by pioneer societies and held at the **Bancroft Library** and **California State Library** are the primary sources.
- **Sea arrivals (Cape Horn / Panama route):** **Ship passenger manifests** for arrivals at San Francisco are held at the **National Archives, Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA**. FamilySearch volume **006601003** covers Port Arrival Registers at Sacramento 1849–1858: 298 images, **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only**. Passenger lists for sea arrivals are partially indexed on Ancestry.com.
- **Naturalizations:** See Court Records above. Pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record at any level.
- **Content note:** Passenger manifests list every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents — examine full manifests when researching a whole family.

### Tax records

- **State and county property tax rolls** began in California at statehood (1850). These are an important substitute for the partially destroyed 1850 census and years between censuses.
- **Where held:** County tax collectors' offices and the **California State Archives**. Limited digitization for the 1850s.
- **Foreign Miners' Tax receipts (1850, 1852):** A distinctive California record — foreign-born miners (particularly Chinese and Latin American) were required to pay a monthly tax; some receipt rolls survive at county recorders' offices and may name individuals otherwise not found in censuses.

### Other record types

- **Voter registration — Great Registers:** California's **Great Registers** (voter registration records) began in **1866** — just outside this target window but essential for tracing men who were in California by the mid-1850s and registered to vote a decade later. FamilySearch collection **California, Great Registers, 1866–1910** (ID 1923340): 1,345,678 records. [Search here](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1923340)
- **Mining company and business records:** Partnership agreements, store ledgers, and assay records — scattered in county recorders' offices, historical societies, and the Bancroft Library.
- **Chinese community records:** Clan association records (tongs), temple registers, and district company files document Chinese miners, though access varies; the **Chinese Historical Society of America** (San Francisco) is the key repository.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | County Births 1850–1919 (789K records); County Marriages 1850–1952 (568K records); Mission Records 1769–1850 (99K records); Great Registers 1866–1910 (1.3M records); 1852 State Census (88% indexed, 522 images); Mining Claim Registers 1849–1855 (browse-only, 340 images); Port Arrival Registers 1849–1858 (browse-only, 298 images) | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census collection (1850, 1860); ship passenger manifests | Subscription |
| **Fold3.com** | Military service records, pension files (NARA-derived) | Subscription |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery transcriptions | Free |
| **Newspapers.com / CDNC** | Historical California newspapers incl. *Alta California* | Subscription / Free (CDNC) |
| **BLM GLO Records** | Federal land patents | Free |
| **NARA Online (Ancestry/Fold3)** | San Francisco passenger manifests, naturalizations | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned **14 digitized volumes** matching California for this period; only the **3 detailed above represent the first page**. Additional volumes exist (nextPageToken present) and were not examined in this survey — consult FamilySearch directly and browse additional pages for further digitized material.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| **National Archives, Pacific Region — San Bruno, CA** | San Francisco passenger manifests; Mexican land grant case files; federal court records incl. naturalizations | In-person; some records on Ancestry |
| **California State Archives, Sacramento** | State census records; state land records; California volunteer military records; legislative records | In-person; some online via [archives.ca.gov](https://www.archives.ca.gov/) |
| **California State Library, Sacramento** | Manuscript collections; Gold Rush diaries; newspaper microfilm; Great Registers on microfilm | In-person; some digitized |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Overland emigrant diaries; Mexican land grant materials; Gold Rush manuscripts; Californio family papers | In-person; some digitized via Calisphere |
| **County courthouses / recorders** (El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Sacramento, etc.) | Deed books; mining claim registers; probate files; marriage registers; tax rolls | In-person or mail request |
| **Chinese Historical Society of America, San Francisco** | Chinese community records, clan association materials | In-person |

---

## Records NOT online

The following records exist for this period but have **no significant online presence** and require in-person or mail access:

- County-level **mining claim registers** (outside San Francisco) at individual county recorders' offices
- Most county **tax rolls** from the 1850s
- County **probate files** from Gold Rush-era mining counties
- Overland emigrant **trail diaries and journals** (held at Bancroft Library and California State Library)
- **Foreign Miners' Tax receipts** (where they survive at county level)
- Chinese **clan association records** (Chinese Historical Society of America)
- **Catholic parish registers** from 1850s mining-town missions (held locally or at diocesan archives)

---

## Known record losses

- **1850 Federal Census:** **Partially destroyed** — some county returns for California are missing (FamilySearch Wiki: *California Genealogy, Pre-Statehood Records*). The 1852 California State Census is the primary substitute.
- **San Francisco fires (1849–1851):** Multiple catastrophic fires destroyed most early San Francisco city records, including many early vital and court records. Substitute with state-level, county-level, or newspaper records.
- **1906 San Francisco Earthquake and Fire:** Though beyond this period, this event later destroyed the NARA Pacific Region records stored in the city — some pre-1906 immigration and court records from that fire are unrecoverable.
- **Mining-camp records:** Transient populations and impermanent settlements meant that many mining-camp records were simply never created or were lost when camps were abandoned.

---

## Research tips

1. **Start with the 1852 California State Census** — this is the single most important Gold Rush-era census substitute, captures the peak migration period, and is 88% name-indexed on FamilySearch. Combine it with the surviving portions of the 1850 federal census.

2. **Work by county, not just by state** — California's Gold Rush counties held most civil records. Identify which county covered your ancestor's location in the specific year of interest, then search that county's collections. County boundaries shifted significantly in the 1850s.

3. **For sea arrivals, check San Francisco passenger manifests** at the National Archives San Bruno and on Ancestry.com. For overland arrivals, there are no formal federal records — look for trail diaries and emigrant compilations at the Bancroft Library and California State Library (FamilySearch Wiki: *California Genealogy, Gold Rush Records*: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)).

4. **Search the *Alta California* newspaper** — arrival and departure notices, partnership announcements, legal notices, and inquests appeared regularly. The California Digital Newspaper Collection (CDNC) offers free full-text search at [cdnc.ucr.edu](https://cdnc.ucr.edu/).

5. **Great Registers begin in 1866** — if your ancestor was in California by the late 1850s, he almost certainly appears in the Great Registers (voter rolls). Though just outside this period, they are an invaluable bridge to confirm identity and residence ([FamilySearch Collection 1923340](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1923340)).

6. **Mining claim registers are browse-only** — the FamilySearch volumes for mining claim registers (and port arrival registers) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. Budget time for image-by-image browsing, or visit county recorders' offices directly.

7. **Follow the ancestor home first** — many '49ers were in California only briefly before returning east. Check the 1850 and 1860 federal censuses in their *home* state as well; naturalization records (pre-1906, filed in any court of record) may appear in either California or the home state.

8. **For Chinese ancestors**, the standard record trail is supplemented by clan association records (Chinese Historical Society of America) and Foreign Miners' Tax receipts at county level — where they survive.

9. **Pre-statehood (1848–1850) records are extremely sparse** — civil infrastructure barely existed. For this narrow window, focus on military district records, early newspaper notices, and the Mission Records collection for any Catholic sacramental events.

10. **The FamilySearch Wiki California Genealogy page** ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy)) is the recommended starting point for additional research strategy detail — the place-specific wiki pages did not load fully through this survey's tools, so consult the wiki directly for the most current guidance.

Additional volumes — likely including more county-level vital, court, and land records — exist and should be explored directly on FamilySearch.

Here is the locality research guide for New York City, colonial 1700s.

---

# 🗽 Locality Research Guide: New York City, 1700s (Colonial Period)

**Jurisdiction:** New York, New York, United States  
**Target Period:** 1700–1800 (British colonial rule, 1664–1783, followed by early American period)  
**Standardized Place:** `New York, New York, United States`  
**FamilySearch Place:** [View on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/en/research/places/?text=New+York+City&focusedId=7023)

---

## Jurisdictional Context

New York City was founded by the Dutch as **New Amsterdam** in 1626 and seized by England in 1664, when it was renamed New York. Throughout the 1700s it served as the capital of **New York Province** under the British Crown — a major commercial port and one of the most populous and ethnically diverse cities in colonial North America.

**Critical framing for 1700s research:**
- **No civil vital registration existed** in the colonial period. There was no government-mandated recording of births, marriages, or deaths. **Church registers are your only vital records substitute.**
- The colonial city was centered on **Manhattan Island**. The modern boroughs (Brooklyn/Kings County, Queens, Staten Island/Richmond County, the Bronx/Westchester) were **separate jurisdictions** with their own record-keeping — do not assume NYC records cover them.
- Colonial-era records split into two periods: **Dutch-legacy records** (Dutch language, Dutch Reformed church dominance, Dutch legal customs in land and probate) and **British-era records** (English, Anglican/Church of England prominence, English common law).

---

## ⛪ Church Records — **HIGHEST PRIORITY**

Since there is no civil registration, church registers are the primary source for births (as baptisms), marriages, and deaths (as burials) throughout the entire 1700s.

### Dutch Reformed Church Registers
- **FamilySearch Digitized Volume:** imageGroupNumber `007733180` — 211 images, covering **New York City, 1700–1776**
- **Access level: Browse-only images. 0% name-indexed. Not full-text searchable.** Must be browsed page by page with no search capability.
- ⚠️ **Language: Dutch (nl).** Reading these registers requires Dutch language ability. Consider the `/translation` skill for assistance.
- Earliest continuous register series in the city, beginning 1639.
- Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — New York City Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

### Broader Church Records Collection (Indexed)
- **FamilySearch Collection:** [New York, Church Records, 1640–1940](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062) (Collection ID: 1469062)
- Date range **1640–1940** — fully covers the target period
- 2,345,678 records with 1,172,839 images; **name-indexed and searchable**
- Covers multiple denominations across the state

### Other Key Denominations to Search
| Denomination | Notes |
|---|---|
| Anglican / Church of England | **Trinity Church** (founded 1697, Manhattan) — baptism, marriage, burial registers; major repository for English colonists |
| Presbyterian | First Presbyterian Church, active from 1716 |
| French Huguenot | L'Église du Saint-Esprit (founded 1628); French-language registers |
| Lutheran | Dutch and German Lutheran congregations |
| Quaker (Friends) | Meeting records at the NY Yearly Meeting archives |
| Jewish | Shearith Israel (Spanish & Portuguese Synagogue, oldest in North America, 1654) — circumcision, marriage, burial records |

**Where to access denominational records beyond FamilySearch:**
- **New-York Historical Society (N-YHS):** https://www.nyhistory.org — holds many original registers
- **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYG&B):** https://www.newyorkfamilyhistory.org — extensive transcriptions and indexes of colonial church records

---

## 🏡 Land Records — **HIGH VALUE**

Land records are a key source for colonial families, as they document property ownership, neighbors (from deeds), and family relationships (from patents/grants).

- **FamilySearch Collection:** [New York, Land Records, 1630–1975](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654) (Collection ID: 2078654)
- Date range **1630–1975** — covers the full target period
- 1,567,890 records with 783,945 images
- Includes deeds, patents, grants, and mortgages
- **New York State Archives (Albany):** Holds colonial-era land patents granted by the Crown/Province governor — essential for 1700s land ownership
- Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — New York City Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

---

## ⚖️ Probate Records — **HIGH VALUE**

Wills and estate inventories name family members, neighbors, and often document enslaved persons.

- **FamilySearch Collection:** [New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780) (Collection ID: 1542780)
- Date range **1629–1971** — covers the full target period
- 987,654 records with 493,827 images
- Colonial-era wills were proved before the **Prerogative Court of New York** (a provincial court with authority over the entire colony)
- **The Abstracts of Wills series**, published by the **New-York Historical Society**, is an essential printed index for colonial-era estates — check this before browsing raw volumes
- Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — New York City Genealogy, Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)

---

## 💰 Tax Records

- **FamilySearch Collection:** [New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432) (Collection ID: 1678432)
- Date range **1799–1804** — touches only the very tail of the target period (1799–1800)
- 123,456 records; **not a prime source for most of the 1700s**
- Earlier colonial tax and ward assessment lists survive at the **New York State Archives** and the **New-York Historical Society** but do not appear as indexed FamilySearch collections — these must be consulted directly at those repositories or via their digitized microfilm

---

## 🏛️ Court Records

Colonial court records frequently name residents in civil suits, debt actions, and criminal matters — a significant substitute when church or vital records are absent.

- **Mayor's Court of New York City** — records for the colonial period
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts** — held at the **New York State Archives, Albany**; documents provincial government actions, land grants, and more
- FamilySearch has no standalone indexed collection for colonial NYC court records in the 1700s — access is via the State Archives directly or through microfilm
- Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — New York City Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

---

## 🎖️ Military Records

Colonial militia rolls are useful for identifying male residents of military age.

- **Colonial militia rolls** list men of military age — held at the NY State Archives; no standalone FamilySearch indexed collection confirmed for this period
- **Fold3:** [https://www.fold3.com/](https://www.fold3.com/) — military records, including Revolutionary War (end of the colonial period)
- **NARA:** [https://www.archives.gov/](https://www.archives.gov/) — federal repository for military pension files and service records (primarily post-1776)
- Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — New York City Genealogy, Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records)

---

## 📰 Newspapers

Colonial newspapers published notices of deaths, marriages, ship arrivals, land sales, and runaway servant/enslaved person notices.

- **New York Gazette** (founded 1725, the city's first newspaper) and **New York Weekly Journal** (founded 1733) — key colonial-era papers
- **Newspapers.com:** [https://www.newspapers.com/](https://www.newspapers.com/) — historical newspaper archives

---

## ⚰️ Cemetery Records

- **Find A Grave:** [https://www.findagrave.com/](https://www.findagrave.com/) — includes Trinity Church burial ground and Dutch Reformed cemeteries
- Trinity Church's burial ground (lower Manhattan) and the Dutch Reformed churchyards are among the oldest surviving burial sites with colonial-era stones

---

## 🔍 Census & Population Enumerations

- There was **no federal census** before 1790 (which postdates most of the colonial period)
- **Provincial censuses** of New York were conducted at irregular intervals during the 1700s — these are held at the NY State Archives and have been partially published
- The **1790 federal census** is the first available and covers New York City at the end of this period

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | Access | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) | Free; church, land, probate collections indexed |
| **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYG&B)** | [newyorkfamilyhistory.org](https://www.newyorkfamilyhistory.org) | Subscription; colonial transcriptions & indexes |
| **New-York Historical Society (N-YHS)** | [nyhistory.org](https://www.nyhistory.org) | On-site & some digital; church registers, Abstracts of Wills |
| **New York State Archives (Albany)** | [archives.nysed.gov](https://archives.nysed.gov) | Colonial Manuscripts, land patents, court records |
| **New York City Municipal Archives** | [nyc.gov/cityrecords](https://www.nyc.gov/site/records/index.page) | City government records (most pre-date modern civil registration) |
| **NARA** | [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov) | Military pension files, post-1776 federal records |
| **Ancestry.com** | [ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com) — subscription | Broad coverage including colonial NY collections |

---

## ⚠️ Key Research Quirks

1. **No civil vital registration in the 1700s.** There was no government birth, marriage, or death registration during this period. Church registers are your only substitute — identify your ancestor's denomination first.

2. **The Dutch Reformed Church volume on FamilySearch (imageGroupNumber 007733180) is browse-only and in Dutch.** It cannot be searched by name and requires Dutch language ability to read. Browse image-by-image at FamilySearch or seek published transcriptions at NYG&B or N-YHS.

3. **Manhattan ≠ all of NYC.** Colonial New York City was Manhattan. Brooklyn, Queens, Staten Island, and the Bronx area were separate counties (Kings, Queens, Richmond, Westchester) with their own church, court, and land records — search those repositories separately if your family may have lived there.

4. **The Prerogative Court probated all provincial wills.** Colonial wills were not handled by county surrogate courts until after independence. Use the *Abstracts of Wills* (New-York Historical Society publication) as your first finding aid.

5. **Dutch legal and linguistic legacy.** Even after 1664, many NYC families continued Dutch naming conventions (patronymics), Dutch-language church records, and Dutch property customs well into the 1700s. Be prepared to search Dutch-language sources and understand patronymic surname shifts (e.g., Jan Pietersen's son Cornelius may be recorded as Cornelius Jansen).

6. **"New York, County Marriages, 1847–1849; 1907–1936" does NOT cover the 1700s.** That FamilySearch collection begins in 1847 — do not rely on it for colonial marriage research.

7. **Tax lists and ward records for most of the 1700s are physical-only.** The FamilySearch tax collection (1799–1804) barely overlaps the target period. Earlier ward-level tax lists exist at the NY State Archives and N-YHS but are not indexed online.

---

# 🗺️ Virginia — Revolutionary War Era (1775–1783)
### Locality Guide: Military Service & Wartime Activities

---

## Jurisdictional Context

**Standard place:** Virginia, United States (State; FamilySearch date range from +1788, reflecting constitutional ratification — though Virginia declared independence in 1776).

The 1775–1783 window straddles **two political eras**: Virginia was the Colony of Virginia under the Crown through mid-1776, then the Commonwealth of Virginia thereafter. Records created before and after July 4, 1776 may be filed under different governmental authorities — colonial vs. state — but county courthouses were the continuous record-keeping unit throughout both eras, making county records the primary research thread.

Virginia maintained **county-level record-keeping from the 1630s**, making it one of the best-documented colonial jurisdictions. However, Virginia had no statewide civil registration of births or deaths during this period — vital events are captured in county court records, parish registers, and church records rather than a central registry.

⚠️ **Critical quirk — missing 1790 federal census:** The Virginia schedules from the first federal census (1790) were destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. The **1782–1785 personal property tax lists** (held at the Library of Virginia and partially digitized on FamilySearch) are the standard substitute and are the earliest post-war population-level source for the state. Plan to use them in lieu of a 1790 census baseline.

⚠️ **County boundary changes:** Virginia created many new counties throughout the 18th century. A family record may be filed under a county that no longer exists, or a county that was the parent of the modern county you're searching. Always identify what county a location belonged to *at the time of the event*, not today.

---

## Record Survey

### 🪖 1. Military Service Records — TIER 1 PRIORITY

These are the most direct evidence of wartime service and should be the first records searched.

| Record Type | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Continental Army service records & muster rolls | NARA, Record Group 93 | Physical + microfilm; some digitized on Fold3 |
| Virginia militia records | Library of Virginia, Richmond | Physical; partial microfilm at FamilySearch |
| Pension & bounty-land warrant applications | NARA, Record Group 15 | Digitized & indexed on Fold3; also FamilySearch |
| Virginia State Navy records (published) | Library of Virginia; published transcripts | Available in print & some digitized |

**FamilySearch collection (from collections_search):**
- **"Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783"** — Collection ID 1945678, date range 1775–1783, 345,678 records, 172,839 images → [Search this collection](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678)

**What these records contain:** Muster rolls list soldiers present at a given time and place; service records document enlistment, rank, unit, and sometimes discharge or death. Pension files (filed post-war, mostly 1818–1855) are genealogically rich — veterans or widows submitted sworn statements of service, family members, and often marriage and birth information.

**Source (FamilySearch Wiki):** Continental Line service records and muster rolls at NARA (RG 93); Virginia militia records at the Library of Virginia; pension and bounty-land warrant applications at NARA (RG 15); and published Virginia State Navy records — all confirmed at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War).

---

### 🌾 2. Bounty Land Records — POST-WAR TRAIL

After the Revolution, Virginia granted bounty lands in the **Virginia Military District of Ohio** to its veterans.

- Warrant and survey records connecting veterans to land claims are held at the **Virginia State Library** (now the Library of Virginia).
- These records are filed in **Ohio**, not Virginia — do not overlook them simply because you are searching Virginia records.
- This is confirmed at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands).

⚠️ **Quirk:** Bounty land warrants for Virginia veterans are split between records at the Library of Virginia (warrants issued) and records in Ohio (where the land was surveyed and granted). Search both.

---

### 📋 3. Tax Lists — Census Substitute

Because the 1790 Virginia federal census was destroyed, the **1782–1785 personal property tax lists** are the primary population-level source for families living in Virginia during and immediately after the war.

**FamilySearch collection (from collections_search):**
- **"Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850"** — Collection ID 1456723, date range 1782–1850, 456,789 records, 228,394 images → [Search this collection](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723)

Tax lists were compiled at the **county level** and typically list adult free white males and their taxable property (land, slaves, livestock, vehicles). Men absent from tax lists may have been away on military service — a negative finding here can itself be evidence of wartime activity.

---

### ⛪ 4. Church Records — Vital Events & Community Ties

Virginia had no statewide vital registration during this period. The Church of England (Anglican/Episcopal) served as the established church of colonial Virginia and maintained **vestry records** recording baptisms, marriages, and burials at the parish level. After the Revolution, the disestablishment of the Anglican church disrupted many parish record series — records may be incomplete for the late 1770s–1780s.

**FamilySearch collection (from collections_search):**
- **"Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929"** — Collection ID 1598230, date range 1680–1929, 1,234,567 records, 617,283 images → [Search this collection](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230)

Also search for:
- **Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian** records, which expanded rapidly in Virginia after the Revolution when religious disestablishment opened the field
- Vestry books and overseers-of-the-poor records (county-level; held at Library of Virginia or county courthouses)

⚠️ **Quirk:** The disestablishment of the Anglican church during the Revolution means many Anglican/Episcopal vestry records have gaps from roughly 1776–1785. If Anglican records are absent for this window, search Baptist and Methodist registers, which were being established in these same years.

---

### 🏡 5. Land, Marriage & Will Records — County Court Trail

County courts were the administrative backbone of Virginia throughout this period. They recorded deeds, marriages, wills, estate inventories, and guardianship — making them the most complete surviving source for family relationships.

**FamilySearch collection (from collections_search):**
- **"Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900"** — Collection ID 1734285, date range 1600–1900, 2,567,890 records, 1,283,945 images → [Search this collection](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285)
- **"Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920"** — Collection ID 2134567, date range 1650–1920, 1,789,012 records, 894,506 images → [Search this collection](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567)

**What to look for with a wartime angle:**
- **Deed books:** Veterans sometimes sold or received land following service; bounty-land deeds can appear in county deed books
- **Will books:** Wills proved during or just after the war may mention military service or wartime debts
- **Orphans' court / guardian records:** Families of men killed in the war appear in guardianship records when minor children needed appointed guardians
- **Estate inventories:** Itemized property lists sometimes include military equipment (muskets, swords) suggesting service

---

### 📰 6. Newspapers — Wartime Context & Names

Historical newspapers can identify soldiers by name (casualty reports, muster calls), document wartime events in specific localities, and occasionally publish Loyalist lists or oath-of-allegiance records.

- **Access:** [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) (subscription) and the Library of Virginia's online newspaper holdings
- Virginia newspapers during this period include the *Virginia Gazette* (Williamsburg), which published throughout the war

---

### 🏛️ Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What it holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Library of Virginia** (Richmond, VA) | Militia records, tax lists, county court microfilm, vestry books, bounty-land warrants, Virginia State Navy records | In-person & online catalog at lva.virginia.gov |
| **National Archives (NARA)** — Washington, DC | Continental Army service records (RG 93), pension & bounty-land files (RG 15) | In-person; Fold3 (digitized) |
| **Fold3.com** | Digitized pension files, compiled service records | Subscription; indexed |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Virginia military, church, land, tax, and court collections (see above) | Free; mixed indexed/browse |
| **Ancestry.com** | Virginia colonial and state records; federal census from 1810 onward | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery records — may document veterans with wartime service inscriptions | Free |

---

### ⚠️ Gaps & Known Limitations

| Gap | Notes |
|---|---|
| **1790 federal census destroyed** | Use 1782–1785 personal property tax lists as substitute |
| **No statewide vital registration** (1775–1783) | Rely on parish/church registers and county court records |

| **FamilySearch Wiki place-specific pages** | The Virginia-specific wiki pages did not return focused content in this session; check [FamilySearch Wiki: Virginia](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Genealogy) directly for the most current research guidance |

### 🔗 External Repositories (from `external_links_search`)

The following FamilySearch-curated external resources are relevant for this period and place:
- [Military Records — Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) — pension files, compiled service records
- [National Archives (NARA)](https://www.archives.gov/) — federal-level service and pension records

## Recommended Search Order

1. **FamilySearch "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783"** (Collection 1945678) — direct hit if your ancestor served

# 📍 Locality Guide: New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana — Early 1800s (c. 1800–1850)
### Focus: Record Survivorship After Disasters & Substitute Sources

---

## Jurisdictional Context

| Period | Governing Authority | Administrative Unit |
|---|---|---|
| 1718–1769 | French colony | Province of Louisiana |
| 1769–1803 | Spanish colony | Provincia de Luisiana |
| 1803–1812 | U.S. Territory of Orleans | Orleans Territory |
| 1812–present | State of Louisiana | Orleans **Parish** |

**Critical quirk:** Louisiana uses **parishes** (not counties) as its primary administrative unit, a legacy of French and Spanish Catholic governance. "Orleans Parish" is the jurisdiction that encompasses New Orleans. Louisiana also inherited a **civil-law legal system** from France and Spain — the only such system in the United States. This means many records have no counterpart elsewhere in the U.S.: successions (not probate), tutorships (not guardianship), interdictions, and notarial acts rather than deed books.

---

## 🔥 Disaster History & Record Losses

This is the central challenge for early New Orleans research. Two events devastated the documentary record:

### The Great Fires of 1788 and 1794
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [New Orleans Genealogy, §Records Surviving Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))*

- **Good Friday Fire, 1788** — destroyed approximately 856 buildings in the French Quarter, including the original St. Louis Cathedral. Many French-era colonial administrative records and early church registers were lost.
- **Second Great Fire, 1794** — destroyed another ~212 buildings, causing further record loss.

Together these fires eliminated most of New Orleans's original French colonial paper trail. What survives from the French period (1718–1769) is fragmentary and largely held at the Louisiana Historical Center or in France.

### Chronic Flooding
New Orleans sits below sea level in a floodplain. While no single flood created record losses as catastrophic as the fires, courthouse basements and local repositories have suffered recurring water damage across two centuries. Microfilming and digitization efforts were partly driven by this ongoing preservation emergency.

---

## ✅ What Survived — Record by Record

### 1. Catholic Sacramental Registers *(Primary vital source)*
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Louisiana Church Records, §Catholic Sacramental Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Church_Records#Catholic))*

The Catholic Church's records are **the single most important vital source** for New Orleans in this period. Louisiana had **no civil registration of births or deaths in the early 1800s** — church registers are what survive in their place.

- **St. Louis Cathedral** (New Orleans): baptisms, marriages, and burials from **1731 to present**, though with gaps corresponding to the 1788 and 1794 fires. Post-fire registers resume with some reconstitution efforts.
- **Other Catholic parish churches** in New Orleans also hold sacramental registers; the Archdiocese of New Orleans holds the collection.
- **Language shifts:** records are in **French (1718–1769)**, **Spanish (1769–1803)**, and **English (after 1803)** — though French continued in common use well into the 1800s. Pre-1803 entries require reading French or Spanish.
- FamilySearch has microfilmed many of these registers. **Collection: [Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)** (collection ID 1612905), which overlaps the full target period.
- **Access note:** Some volumes are browse-only. Non-English entries require translation.
- **Free people of color (gens de couleur libres):** This population — a legally recognized third status unique to antebellum Louisiana — often appears in **separate sections** of sacramental registers. Check both the "white" and "free colored" sections.

---

### 2. Notarial Archives *(Primary substitute for deeds, wills, contracts)*
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Louisiana Genealogy, §Notarial Archives](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Notarial_Archives))*

This is arguably the richest surviving substitute for destroyed civil records. Under Louisiana's civil-law system, **notarial acts** — not deed books or county court records — are where you find:
- Property sales and transfers
- Marriage contracts (often recording both families' assets)
- Successions (equivalent of probate — wills, inventories, heirs)
- Tutorships (guardianship of minors)
- Emancipation of enslaved persons
- Slave sales and transactions

**New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds **over 30 million pages** of notarial acts from **1733 to the present**.

**⚠️ Critical access quirk:** Notarial records are **organized by notary's name and date**, not by the names of parties to the act. You must know an approximate date and the acting notary's name to search effectively. Name indexes exist for some periods but are incomplete.

**Colonial-era notarial records** (French: 1718–1769; Spanish: 1769–1803) are **not** at the Notarial Archives Research Center — they are held at the **Louisiana Historical Center** in the Old U.S. Mint building.

**On FamilySearch:** Volume search returned **1 digitized volume** of Orleans Parish Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies), covering **1803–1820**, consisting of **167 browse-only images** in French and English (imageGroupNumber: 004990115). This volume is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — it must be browsed page by page. No further volumes covering 1820–1850 were returned, representing a digitization gap for that later period.

---

### 3. Succession Records *(Louisiana's version of probate)*
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Louisiana Genealogy, §Parish System](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System))*

- Successions are filed in Louisiana civil district courts (at the parish level, not through a separate probate court).
- The **Louisiana State Archives** in Baton Rouge holds territorial and early state records.
- **FamilySearch Collection: [Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)** (collection ID 2078341) — covers the full target period. Check FamilySearch's catalog for current indexing and image counts.
- Succession files typically include inventories of personal property — including, for enslaved people, their first names and sometimes ages — making them valuable for researching both white and Black New Orleans families.

---

### 4. Federal Census Records
The federal census is a key substitute when vital records are absent or destroyed.

| Year | Coverage Notes |
|---|---|
| 1800 | Louisiana was not yet a U.S. state; territorial population schedules are incomplete |
| 1810 | First full enumeration including Orleans Territory; names heads of household only |
| 1820 | Names heads of household; includes free colored column |
| 1830 | Names heads of household |
| 1840 | Names heads of household |
| 1850 | First census naming all free household members individually — a major resource |

The 1850 census is the first to name all individuals, making it especially useful as a landmark record after which other records can be traced backward.

---

### 5. Marriage Records
- **Primary source (1800–1837):** Catholic sacramental marriage registers — see §1 above.
- **FamilySearch Collection: [Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1798054)** (collection ID 1798054) — begins in 1837, so it **does not cover 1800–1836**. For that window, church registers are your only systematic source.

---

### 6. Death Records
- No civil death registration existed in Louisiana in the early 1800s. Catholic burial registers are the primary source.
- **FamilySearch Collection: [Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892)** (collection ID 1543892) — begins 1819, but coverage before statewide registration began is spotty; early entries likely derive from church or newspaper sources rather than civil registration.

---

### 7. Land Records
- For the early American period (post-1803), federal land patents in Louisiana are searchable at the **BLM General Land Office** website (glorecords.blm.gov).
- Property **transfers** between private parties go through notarial acts (see §2), not deed books.
- Spanish land grants from the colonial era are held at the **Louisiana State Land Office** and some are at the Louisiana Historical Center.

---

### 8. Immigration & Passenger Lists *(Major substitute and corroborating source)*
New Orleans was **one of the busiest ports of entry in 19th-century America** — second only to New York for much of the antebellum period. Enormous numbers of European, Caribbean, and South American immigrants arrived here.

- Passenger arrival lists are held at **NARA** and are searchable on Ancestry.com, FamilySearch, and Fold3.
- For immigrants who arrived at New Orleans and then moved inland, this is often the **first American record** of a family.

---

### 9. Military Records
- **War of 1812 / Battle of New Orleans (January 8, 1815):** Many New Orleans residents served. Service records and pension files are at NARA; Fold3 has digitized much of this material.
- Louisiana militia and volunteer unit records may be at the Louisiana State Archives.

---

### 10. Newspapers *(Substitute for announcements, deaths, marriages)*
New Orleans had an active multi-lingual press by the early 1800s (*Louisiana Gazette*, *Le Courrier de la Louisiane*, etc.). Newspapers published:
- Death notices and obituaries
- Marriage announcements
- Estate and succession notices (legally required)
- Runaway-slave advertisements (important for enslaved-ancestor research)

Access: **Newspapers.com** and the **Library of Congress Chronicling America** project (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) hold historical New Orleans newspaper issues.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts, 1733–present (American period) | In-person; partial digitization |
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint) | Colonial notarial records, French/Spanish periods (1718–1803) | In-person |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans | Catholic sacramental registers, 1731–present | Contact archdiocese; FamilySearch microfilm |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and early state records, successions, land | In-person; partial online |
| NARA (National Archives) | Federal census, passenger lists, military | archives.gov; Ancestry; FamilySearch |
| FamilySearch.org | Church records, probate, notarial (partial) | Online; browse-only for many volumes |
| BLM GLO | Federal land patents | glorecords.blm.gov (free, online) |
| Newspapers.com / Chronicling America | Historical newspapers | Online subscriptions / free |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | findagrave.com (free) |

---

## Key Research Quirks for Early New Orleans

1. **The 1788 and 1794 fires destroyed most French colonial records** — do not expect pre-1769 parish records to be intact. Work from notarial archives and surviving church registers.
2. **Catholic church records are your vital-records substitute** for the entire early 1800s — Louisiana had no statewide civil registration in this period.
3. **Notarial archives are organized by notary name + date, not by party name** — you need an approximate date and notary to search effectively. Colonial records (pre-1803) are at the Louisiana Historical Center, not the Notarial Archives Research Center.
4. **Language:** Records shift from French → Spanish → English across 1769 and 1803. French remained in common use well into the 1800s. Pre-1803 records require reading French or Spanish.
5. **"Succession" ≠ "probate"; "tutorship" ≠ "guardianship"** — use Louisiana civil-law terminology when searching catalogs.
6. **Free people of color appear in separate register sections** — check both sections of sacramental registers. This legally distinct population left records in most major New Orleans record types.
7. **The 1850 federal census is a landmark** — it first names all free household members individually, allowing backward reconstruction of family chronology.
8. **New Orleans was a major immigration port** — passenger lists often survive when local records do not. Check arrivals even if the family didn't stay in New Orleans.
9. **The volume_search returned only 1 digitized FamilySearch volume** (Orleans Parish Notarial Acts, 1803–1820, 167 images) — coverage for 1820–1850 notarial records on FamilySearch appears to be a gap; researchers should contact the Notarial Archives Research Center directly for that window.

---

## Digitization Levels at a Glance

| Record Type | FamilySearch Availability | Access Mode |
|---|---|---|
| Church Records, 1718–1925 | Collection 1612905 | Indexed + images (verify in catalog) |
| Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 | Collection 1798054 | Indexed + images |
| Probate/Successions, 1756–1984 | Collection 2078341 | Indexed + images |
| Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 | Collection 1543892 | Index only (0 images) |
| Notarial Acts (Orleans), 1803–1820 | 1 volume, 167 images | **Browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text) |
| Notarial Acts (Orleans), 1820–1850 | Not found in volume search | Likely physical/microfilm only — contact repository |
| Colonial notarial records, pre-1803 | Not returned | Physical at Louisiana Historical Center |

---

**Bottom line for your research:** The fires of 1788 and 1794 are real losses, but New Orleans's civil-law infrastructure left a remarkably rich parallel paper trail in **notarial archives and Catholic church registers** that partially compensates. For the early 1800s target window, lead with the **Archdiocese sacramental registers** (via FamilySearch Collection 1612905) and the **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** for any property, succession, or contract event. Supplement with federal census records and — for immigrant ancestors — New Orleans passenger lists, which are often the first surviving American record of a family.

# Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — Port of Entry Immigration (1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **City:** Boston — established as a town 1630; incorporated as a city 1822
- **County:** Suffolk County — one of the original Massachusetts Bay Colony counties, formed 1643
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Massachusetts (admitted to the Union 1788)
- **Population during period:** By 1850, over one-quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born, reflecting the massive surge of Famine-era immigration [(Wikipedia: Boston)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston)
- **Economy:** Maritime trade, commerce, textile manufacturing; Boston was one of the five major US ports of entry in the 1840s [(FamilySearch Wiki: Massachusetts Immigration)](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)
- **Ethnic composition:** Established Yankee Protestant population receiving enormous waves of Irish Catholic immigrants (especially 1845–1852); smaller numbers of German and other European arrivals
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist, Episcopal, and Methodist (established community); Roman Catholic parishes multiplying rapidly to serve Irish arrivals; Baptist and Quaker congregations also present
- **Key historical events:** Irish Potato Famine (1845–1852) drove the defining immigration wave; Boston was one of the closest major American ports to Ireland

## Boundary changes
- **Critical research gotcha:** In the 1840s the city of Boston was confined to the original Shawmut Peninsula. The surrounding communities — **Roxbury, Charlestown, Dorchester, Brighton, and West Roxbury** — were entirely separate towns under their own jurisdictions. An immigrant who arrived at Boston but settled across the street in Roxbury generated vital records, tax records, and church records under *Roxbury*, not Boston. These towns were not annexed until Roxbury (1868), Dorchester (1870), Charlestown (1874), Brighton and West Roxbury (1874). Search those towns' records independently for the 1840s.
- East Boston (Noddle's Island / East Boston neighborhood) was being actively developed in the 1840s as an arrival point for immigrants — its records may appear under East Boston or under Boston proper depending on the record type.
- Suffolk County boundaries were stable throughout this period.

---

## Available record types

### Immigration / passenger lists — **Primary source**
- **Record series:** Customs passenger lists (arrival manifests) for the Port of Boston, 1820–1891 — National Archives Record Group 36 [(FamilySearch Wiki: Massachusetts Immigration)](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)
- **Content of 1840s lists:** Name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin only. Unlike post-1892 Ellis Island manifests, 1840s customs lists do **not** record the immigrant's town of origin, last residence, or US contact. Examine the full manifest page for traveling companions — infants and young children are listed alongside parents.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891 (id: 1784312) — [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312) — 1,234,567 records
- **Digitized volume:** Image group **003345210**, "Passenger Lists, Port of Boston," 1840–1850 — 389 images. This volume is **full-text searchable but only 3% name-indexed.** Do not rely on the FamilySearch name index for 1840–1850 arrivals — use full-text search or browse the 389 images directly. A name-index miss does *not* mean the person was absent. This is the complete digitized volume set returned for Boston, 1820–1870 (totalResults: 1).
- **Physical originals:** National Archives at Boston, 380 Trapelo Road, Waltham, MA — holds original NARA RG 36 customs passenger lists [(FamilySearch Wiki: Massachusetts Immigration)](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)
- **Also on Ancestry:** The Massachusetts Passenger Lists collection is indexed and searchable on Ancestry.com (subscription)

### Naturalization records
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906 (id: 1459213) — [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213) — 345,678 records
- **Jurisdictional note:** Before 1906, any court of record could naturalize immigrants — the US District Court for Massachusetts, the Suffolk County Superior Court, county courts of common pleas, and even some municipal courts. Search all courts, not just federal ones.
- **Two documents to seek:**
  - *Declaration of Intention* ("first papers") — filed shortly after arrival; states arrival date and country of origin
  - *Petition for Naturalization* — filed after a waiting period (2–5 years); may name witnesses who can lead to additional family connections
- **Physical holdings:** National Archives at Boston (Waltham) for federal court records; Massachusetts Archives for state court naturalizations

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Town-level registration (from 1639):** Massachusetts town clerks were ordered by the General Court to record births, marriages, and deaths beginning in 1639. Boston's town/city clerk records therefore far predate the statewide system.
- **Statewide registration (from 1841):** Massachusetts established statewide centralized vital registration in 1841 — meaning the 1840s sits at the *very start* of state-level records. Early statewide records (1841–1844 especially) may be incomplete.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890 (id: 2061550) — [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) — 3,456,789 records
- **Neighboring towns:** Search Roxbury, Charlestown, and Dorchester town vital records separately — they are not part of Boston's records in this period

### Church records
- **Primary importance for Irish immigrants:** Catholic parish records are the essential supplement to civil registration. Baptisms, marriages, and burials were recorded in parish registers as Irish Catholic parishes multiplied from the late 1830s through the 1840s.
- **Key Boston parishes:** Cathedral of the Holy Cross (central Boston) and St. Patrick's (East Boston) are among the earliest Catholic parishes serving Irish immigrants [(FamilySearch Wiki: Massachusetts Church Records)](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)
- **Physical holding:** Archdiocese of Boston Archives, 66 Brooks Drive, Braintree, MA — holds Catholic parish registers [(FamilySearch Wiki: Massachusetts Church Records)](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920 (id: 1921657) — [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) — 987,654 records (covers some but not all parishes; consult the Archdiocese directly for gaps)
- **Non-Catholic denominations:** Protestant church records (Congregational, Episcopal, Baptist) are held at the Massachusetts Historical Society and in the same FamilySearch collection

### Census records
- **1840 federal census (names heads of household only):** Other household members appear as age/sex tally marks — an immigrant who arrived in 1838 is not named as an individual, only counted. Use to establish who headed the household.
- **1850 federal census (first to name every individual):** The key snapshot at the height of Famine immigration. Records name, age, sex, occupation, birthplace (country only — "Ireland"), and real estate value. The 1850 census is fully indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **1850 mortality schedule:** Records deaths in June 1849–May 1850 with cause of death, birthplace, and occupation — valuable for immigrants who died shortly after arrival (typhus and ship fever were common).

### Probate records
- **FamilySearch collection:** Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991 (id: 1678901) — [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) — 567,890 records
- **Jurisdictional level:** Suffolk County Probate Court (Boston)
- **Value for immigrant research:** Even modest estates generated probate files naming next of kin — sometimes including relatives still in Ireland

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Massachusetts is a state-land state)
- **Where held:** Suffolk County Registry of Deeds (Boston); online at [https://www.masslandrecords.com/](https://www.masslandrecords.com/) — free access
- **Note:** Many newly arrived immigrants in the 1840s were renters, not property owners — land records may not appear until later years

### Military records
- **Relevant conflict:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); some Irish immigrants enlisted
- **Where held:** NARA (service records), Massachusetts State Archives (state militia records), Fold3.com (subscription)

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Holy Cross Cemetery (Malden), St. Patrick Cemetery (Lowell), and various Boston municipal cemeteries served the Irish Catholic community
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave ([https://www.findagrave.com/](https://www.findagrave.com/)) — free; BillionGraves

### Newspaper records
- **The Pilot (Boston):** Irish Catholic weekly newspaper — published "Missing Persons" advertisements from the 1840s onward in which recent immigrants sought separated family members. The **Boston College Boston Pilot Missing Persons Database** at [infowanted.bc.edu](http://infowanted.bc.edu) indexes over 40,000 of these notices and is searchable free — often the fastest route to an arrival date and Irish county of origin [(Wikipedia: Boston)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston)
- **Other Boston papers:** Boston Daily Atlas, Boston Herald, Boston Post — marriage notices, death notices, and legal advertisements
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription); Boston Public Library holds extensive newspaper microfilm holdings

### Tax records
- **City of Boston annual property tax assessments** can substitute for census data in non-census years and confirm an immigrant's Boston address between 1840 and 1850
- **Where held:** City of Boston Archives; some records on FamilySearch microfilm (not fully indexed)

## Records NOT online
- Original Catholic parish registers for many 1840s Boston parishes — the FamilySearch Church Records collection (id: 1921657) covers some but not all; consult the Archdiocese of Boston Archives directly
- Suffolk County Superior Court naturalization case files — physical at Massachusetts Archives

## Known record losses
- No major courthouse fire or disaster affecting Suffolk County's core records for the 1840s is identified by the tools consulted. However, individual parish record losses are possible — confirm with the Archdiocese of Boston Archives for specific parishes before concluding a register is missing.

## Research tips
- **Start with The Pilot Missing Persons Database** ([infowanted.bc.edu](http://infowanted.bc.edu)): free, indexed, and regularly the fastest route to a confirmed arrival date and Irish county or townland of origin for Famine-era immigrants.
- **Use full-text search for the 1840–1850 passenger list volume** (image group 003345210): with only 3% name-indexed, a standard name search will miss most arrivals — use FamilySearch's full-text search feature or browse the 389 images directly [(FamilySearch Wiki: Massachusetts Immigration)](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston).
- **1840s passenger lists record limited information** — name, age, sex, occupation, country of origin only. Cross-reference with church records and The Pilot to add geographic precision within Ireland.
- **Search adjacent-town records separately:** Roxbury, Charlestown, East Boston, Dorchester, and South Boston were outside or on the edges of Boston city limits in the 1840s. Vital records and tax records for those areas are separate from Boston's city records.
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations appear in multiple courts:** Search FamilySearch collection 1459213 *and* the Massachusetts Archives for state court naturalizations in addition to federal court records. Any court of record could naturalize in this period.
- **Massachusetts statewide vital registration began in 1841** — the very start of the target decade; early statewide records may be incomplete. Supplement with town clerk records (going back to 1639 at the town level) and Catholic parish registers.
- **Chain migration:** Once an immigrant is located in the 1850 federal census, examine every neighbor in surrounding households — Famine-era Irish immigrants frequently came from the same parish in Ireland and settled near each other in Boston.

# Locality Guide: Boston, Massachusetts — Port of Entry Immigration (1840s)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **City:** Boston — established as a town 1630; incorporated as a city 1822
- **County:** Suffolk County — one of the original Massachusetts Bay Colony counties, formed 1643
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Commonwealth of Massachusetts (admitted to the Union 1788)
- **Population during period:** By 1850, over one-quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born, reflecting the massive surge of Famine-era immigration
- **Economy:** Maritime trade, commerce, textile manufacturing; Boston was one of the five major US ports of entry in the 1840s
- **Ethnic composition:** Established Yankee Protestant population receiving enormous waves of Irish Catholic immigrants (especially 1845-1852); smaller numbers of German and other European arrivals
- **Key historical events:** Irish Potato Famine (1845-1852) drove the defining immigration wave; Boston was one of the closest major American ports to Ireland

## Boundary changes
- In the 1840s Boston was confined to the Shawmut Peninsula. Roxbury, Charlestown, Dorchester, Brighton, and West Roxbury were entirely separate towns — immigrants settling there generated records under those jurisdictions, not Boston. They were annexed 1868-1874.

## Available record types

### Immigration / passenger lists — Primary source
- Customs passenger lists (NARA RG 36), Port of Boston, 1820-1891
- 1840s content: name, age, sex, occupation, country of origin only
- FamilySearch collection 1784312; image group 003345210 (1840-1850, 389 images, 3% indexed, full-text searchable)
- Physical originals: National Archives at Boston, Waltham, MA
- Also indexed on Ancestry.com

### Naturalization records
- FamilySearch collection 1459213 (1790-1906)
- Pre-1906: any court of record could naturalize — search federal, state, and municipal courts
- Declaration of Intention + Petition for Naturalization are separate documents; both valuable
- Physical: NARA Waltham (federal); Massachusetts Archives (state courts)

### Vital records
- Town-level registration from 1639 by order of the General Court
- Statewide registration began 1841; early records may be incomplete
- FamilySearch collection 2061550 (1620-1890, 3,456,789 records)
- Search neighboring towns (Roxbury, Charlestown, Dorchester) separately

### Church records
- Catholic parish registers essential for Irish immigrants; key parishes: Cathedral of the Holy Cross, St. Patrick's (East Boston)
- Archdiocese of Boston Archives, Braintree, MA
- FamilySearch collection 1921657 (1630-1920, 987,654 records; not all parishes included)

### Census records
- 1840 federal census: names heads of household only
- 1850 federal census: first to name all individuals; key snapshot of Famine immigration
- 1850 mortality schedule: records deaths June 1849-May 1850 with birthplace and cause

### Probate records
- FamilySearch collection 1678901 (1635-1991, 567,890 records)
- Suffolk County Probate Court level

### Land records
- Metes and bounds; state-land state
- Suffolk County Registry of Deeds; online at masslandrecords.com (free)

### Newspaper records
- The Pilot (Boston Irish Catholic weekly): Missing Persons Database at infowanted.bc.edu (free, 40,000+ notices indexed) — fastest route to arrival date and Irish county of origin
- Boston Daily Atlas, Boston Herald, Boston Post

### Tax records
- City of Boston annual property assessments; substitute for off-census years
- City of Boston Archives; some on FamilySearch microfilm

## Repository guide

### Online
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Collections 1784312, 1459213, 2061550, 1921657, 1678901 | Free |
| Ancestry.com | Passenger lists, census, naturalizations | Subscription |
| infowanted.bc.edu | Boston Pilot Missing Persons Database | Free |
| masslandrecords.com | Suffolk County deeds | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Boston papers | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives at Boston (Waltham) | NARA RG 36 passenger lists; federal court naturalizations | In-person / online ordering |
| Massachusetts Archives | Statewide vitals from 1841; state court naturalizations | In-person |
| Archdiocese of Boston Archives, Braintree | Catholic parish registers | By appointment |
| City of Boston Archives | Vital records; tax assessments; city directories | In-person |
| Massachusetts Historical Society | Non-Catholic church records; family papers | In-person |
| Boston Public Library | Newspaper microfilm; city directories | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Most original Catholic parish registers for 1840s Boston parishes
- Suffolk County Superior Court naturalization case files
- City of Boston tax assessment books 1840-1849
- Coroner's inquest records for the 1840s

## Research tips
- Start with The Pilot Missing Persons Database (infowanted.bc.edu) — free and indexed
- Use full-text search for passenger list image group 003345210 (3% name-indexed only)
- Search adjacent-town vital and church records separately from Boston's
- Check multiple courts for pre-1906 naturalizations
- Chain migration: examine all neighbors in 1850 census — Famine-era Irish often came from the same Irish parish
