# Locality Guide: Indian Territory / Oklahoma (c. 1830–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview

In the mid-1800s, the land now called Oklahoma was **Indian Territory** — a federally administered region, not a U.S. state. It had no county system, no civil vital registration, and no standard federal census enumeration. Jurisdiction was exercised by two parallel authorities:

- **The federal government** — through the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA/OIA), treaty-making authority, and the U.S. Army
- **Tribal sovereign nations** — the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Muscogee/Creek, and Seminole) each operated their own courts, schools, laws, and record systems

The Indian Removal Act of 1830 forced relocation from the southeastern U.S. via the Trail of Tears; most removals occurred 1830–1842. Oklahoma did not achieve statehood until 1907. The FamilySearch place database lists "Oklahoma, United States" with a start date of 1907 — records before that date are indexed under **"Indian Territory"** in the digitized volume database; search both.

- **Administrative structure:** No counties — governed by tribal territories and BIA agencies
- **Ethnic composition:** Five Civilized Tribes; Plains tribes in the west; "Freedmen" (freed enslaved people of tribal members); some intermarried Euro-Americans and licensed traders
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries active from the 1820s onward ([FamilySearch Wiki: Oklahoma Native American Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records))
- **Key events:** Indian Removal Act 1830; Trail of Tears 1830–1842; Civil War (Indian Territory split, major fighting); post-war reconstruction treaties 1866 (Freedmen granted tribal citizenship)

---

## Boundary changes

| Date | Change | Research implication |
|------|--------|---------------------|
| 1830 | Indian Territory established — covers present-day Oklahoma plus parts of Kansas/Nebraska | Use "Indian Territory" as place in all searches |
| 1854–1867 | Kansas and Nebraska territories carved off the northern section | Northern ancestors may have records in KS/NE archives |
| 1866 | Post-Civil War treaties reorganized tribal lands; Freedmen enrolled | Separate Freedmen rolls begin; search both citizen-by-blood and Freedmen series |
| 1890 | Oklahoma Territory organized from western Indian Territory; Indian Territory (east, Five Civilized Tribes) remains separate | Western-territory families may appear in Oklahoma Territory records from 1890 |
| 1907 | Statehood — Indian Territory and Oklahoma Territory merge | County records begin only at this point |

**Critical quirk:** Searching Oklahoma county records will return nothing for mid-1800s Indian Territory — county government did not exist there during this period.

---

## Available record types

### ⭐ Tribal enrollment rolls — primary source

The most important record class for this period and the functional census substitute throughout. Multiple series exist by tribe:

| Roll | Date | Tribe(s) | Notes |
|------|------|----------|-------|
| Various pre-removal rolls | 1817–1835 | Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole | Created in the Southeast before removal |
| Old Settler Cherokee Roll | 1851 | Cherokee (Western) | Pre-removal settlers already in Indian Territory |
| Drennen Roll | 1852 | Cherokee | Post-removal emigrants |
| Various Choctaw, Creek, Seminole rolls | 1830s–1880s | Tribe-specific | See NARA RG 75 finding aids |
| Dawes Rolls | 1898–1914 | Five Civilized Tribes | Most comprehensive; post-period but records birth years back to 1820s–1870s |

**What they contain:** Name, age, sex, blood quantum, family relationships, tribal affiliation; some note birthplace in the Southeast (before removal).

**FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* — 567,890 records, 283,945 images, indexed and searchable by name ([FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432))

**Digitized volume:** FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume of Tribal Enrollment Cards (imageGroupNumber 002298871) covering Indian Territory 1840–1870, 940 images, **99% name-indexed and full-text searchable** — the most accessible mid-period roll set found in the volume survey.

**Also:** Dawes Rolls and related allotment records indexed on Ancestry. Earlier roll series may require NARA access.

**NARA:** Original records in **Record Group 75** (Bureau of Indian Affairs), National Archives at Fort Worth, TX. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls))

> **Strategy:** Even though the Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) post-date your target period, start there — they are the most thoroughly indexed gateway and record birth years reaching into the 1840s–1870s. From a Dawes entry, trace backward to the 1851, 1852, and earlier rolls.

---

### BIA agency records (annuity rolls, correspondence, school records)

The Office/Bureau of Indian Affairs maintained:
- **Annuity payment rolls** — annual lists of tribal members receiving treaty annuities; the closest thing to an annual census for mid-1800s Indian Territory
- **Agency correspondence** — letters between BIA field agents and Washington naming individuals, families, and events
- **Indian school and mission school records** — enrollment registers for students

**Where held:** National Archives, Washington D.C. (RG 75, OIA Letters Received/Sent); NARA Fort Worth for regional agency records. Partially digitized on Ancestry and FamilySearch. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records))

**Access level:** Mostly **physical only** for pre-1880 correspondence; some annuity rolls on microfilm at the Family History Library (FHL).

---

### Treaties

U.S. treaties with tribal nations document territory boundaries, citizenship, land cessions, and annuity rights. Some treaties list tribal leaders by name; related schedules and claims lists name ordinary tribal members.

**Where held:**
- Originals: National Archives, Washington D.C. (RG 11, General Records of the U.S. Government)
- Transcriptions: *Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties*, compiled by Charles Kappler — digitized free at [Oklahoma State University Digital Collections](https://dc.library.okstate.edu/digital/collection/kapplers)
- NARA online catalog: [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov)

---

### Land and allotment records

**FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907* — 234,567 records, 117,283 images, indexed ([FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872))

In the mid-1800s, land in Indian Territory was held **communally by tribal nations** — individual patents did not exist until the Dawes Act (1887). Mid-period land records include:
- **Improvement records** — documented individual farms/homesteads within tribal territory
- **Permits and licenses** — for non-citizen residents (traders, intermarried whites)
- **Allotment files (post-1887)** — contain family affidavits tracing relationships back to the mid-1800s

**Survey system:** Not the standard U.S. rectangular survey — tribal territories used their own internal boundary systems.

**NARA:** Allotment records in RG 75 at Fort Worth; early land records in RG 49 (GLO) in Washington.

---

### Missionary and church records

Christian missionaries were active in Indian Territory from the 1820s onward. Denominations: Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Moravian. Records include baptism, marriage, and burial registers, plus school enrollment.

**FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965* — 123,456 records, 61,728 images, indexed ([FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321))

**Physical holdings:** Denominational archives hold additional records:
- American Baptist Historical Society
- United Methodist Archives & History Center
- Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia — some digitized)

([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records))

---

### Census records

**No standard federal census covered Indian Territory** — tribal citizens were excluded from the 1830–1880 federal enumerations. Substitutes:
- **Tribal rolls and annuity rolls** (see above) — primary substitutes
- **1880 federal census:** Non-citizen residents of Indian Territory (licensed traders, intermarried whites) DO appear. Some agency-specific Indian enumerations were also taken in 1880.
- **Special Indian census schedules (1885 onward):** Annual BIA censuses begin 1885 — post-period, but useful for families still in place

---

### Military records

Indian Territory saw major Civil War engagement. Many tribal members served on both sides:
- **Confederate:** Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, and Seminole Mounted Rifles and Battalions
- **Union:** Indian Home Guards (multi-tribal units)

Service records are held at NARA; partially indexed and imaged at [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com). **Pension files** at NARA often contain detailed affidavits from family members and can carry biographical information tracing back to the 1840s–1850s.

---

### Tribal newspapers

Indian Territory produced several tribal-language and English newspapers in the target period:
- *Cherokee Phoenix* (founded 1828 in Georgia; continued in Indian Territory)
- *Cherokee Advocate* (Tahlequah, 1844 onward)
- *Indian Journal* (Muskogee area)

These published legal notices, court proceedings, death notices, and community news — often the **only surviving non-enrollment record** for a mid-1800s individual.

**Access:** [Chronicling America / Library of Congress](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov); Oklahoma Historical Society; [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com)

---

### Vital records (civil registration)

**None existed in Indian Territory before statehood (1907).** There was no government mandate for births, marriages, or deaths. Use tribal rolls, church registers, annuity rolls, and BIA correspondence as substitutes. The *Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995* collection on FamilySearch (456,789 records) covers post-statehood marriages only.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Key collections for Indian Territory, mid-1800s | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* (567,890 records); *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907* (234,567 records); *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965* (123,456 records); 1 digitized volume of Tribal Enrollment Cards 1840–1870 (940 images, 99% indexed, full-text searchable) | Free |
| **Ancestry** | Dawes Rolls; various tribal rolls; 1880 federal census for Indian Territory non-citizens | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Civil War service records including Indian Territory units | Subscription |

---

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |

---

## Records NOT online

- Most BIA agency correspondence (pre-1880, RG 75 Letters Received/Sent) — physical at NARA Washington
- Tribal court records for the Five Civilized Tribes — held by tribal archives or Oklahoma Historical Society; largely undigitized for the mid-1800s
- Annuity payment rolls for many agencies — microfilmed at the Family History Library but limited online indexing
- *Cherokee Advocate* and other tribal newspaper issues (especially pre-1870) — microfilm at Oklahoma Historical Society and Library of Congress
- Pre-removal records (created in Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi before 1838) — held in those states' archives, not Oklahoma

---

## Known record losses

- **Civil War destruction (1861–1865):** Indian Territory experienced intense warfare; many tribal government records, school registers, and missionary records were destroyed — particularly in Cherokee and Creek territories
- **Trail of Tears (1838–1842):** Records from life in the Southeast were largely left behind or lost during the forced removal itself
- **Tribal archive losses:** Systematic preservation of smaller tribal records was inconsistent

**Substitutes when rolls are missing:** Annuity payment rolls → missionary baptism/marriage registers → military pension family affidavits → post-war Freedmen's Bureau records (for Freedmen of the Five Civilized Tribes) → tribal newspaper notices

---

## Research tips

1. **Start with the tribe, not the place.** Indian Territory records are organized by tribal affiliation, not county or geography. Determine the ancestor's tribe first, then find the roll series for that tribe. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Oklahoma Native American Records – Tribal Rolls](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls))

2. **Work backward from the Dawes Rolls.** Even though the Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) post-date your target period, they are the most thoroughly indexed source and record birth years reaching back to the 1840s–1870s. Use them as the entry point, then trace to earlier rolls (Old Settler 1851, Drennen 1852, etc.). ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls))

3. **Search "Indian Territory," not Oklahoma counties.** County government did not exist in Indian Territory during the mid-1800s. All FamilySearch and Ancestry searches should use "Indian Territory" as the place.

4. **Check Freedmen rolls separately.** After the 1866 post-Civil War treaties, former enslaved people of tribal members gained citizenship in tribal nations. They were enrolled on separate "Freedmen" rolls — distinct from "citizen by blood" rolls. If your ancestor may have been a Freedman, search both series.

5. **NARA Fort Worth is the primary physical repository.** All Five Civilized Tribes records — Dawes Rolls, land allotment files, agency records — are centered there. Budget for a research trip or engage a local genealogist if key records are not yet digitized.

6. **Check pre-removal records in southeastern states.** If your ancestor was removed from Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, or Tennessee, vital evidence of their life before removal survives in those states' archives — not in Oklahoma.

7. **Blood quantum ≠ enrollment.** Tribal rolls document blood quantum, but tribal citizenship was a separate legal determination. People with significant Indian ancestry were sometimes excluded from rolls (contested citizenship); others with less-documented ancestry were enrolled. Research the citizenship determination files, not just the roll listings.

8. **Use tribal newspapers for individuals absent from formal records.** The *Cherokee Advocate* (1844 onward) published legal notices, court proceedings, death notices, and community announcements that can name individuals who appear nowhere in enrollment records. Access via the Oklahoma Historical Society or Chronicling America.

---

A few key takeaways for your research:

- **The Dawes Rolls are your gateway** even for mid-1800s ancestors — start there, use the recorded birth years to identify earlier rolls
- **NARA Fort Worth holds the core physical collection** — RG 75 is indispensable for anything not yet digitized

- **Annuity rolls are the census substitute** for years when tribal rolls were not taken — they're often overlooked but filed annually

---

## Pennsylvania Quaker Community Records — Locality Guide
**Period:** Late 1700s (c. 1750–1810) | **Place:** Pennsylvania, United States

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Pennsylvania was founded in 1682 by William Penn as a Quaker haven, and it predates statehood (Pennsylvania ratified the Constitution in 1787). For the late 1700s your research spans **both colonial Pennsylvania (~1750–1776) and early statehood (1776–1810)**. No statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in Pennsylvania until **1906** — Quaker meeting records are therefore **the primary substitute for vital registration** throughout this entire period. The heaviest Quaker concentrations were in **Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties**, though meetings also existed in Lancaster, York, and other counties by mid-century.

> **⚠️ Coverage note:** The FamilySearch Wiki place pages for Pennsylvania returned only generic content rather than Pennsylvania-specific guidance on all four sections (home, getting started, online records, research tips). Claims below are grounded in the wiki_search results and tool data; check the FamilySearch Wiki directly at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records) for the full article.

---

### 1. Quaker Meeting Records — The Core Source

Quaker (Society of Friends) meetings kept **meticulous multi-layered records** organized in a hierarchy:

| Level | Scope | What was recorded |
|---|---|---|
| **Monthly Meeting** | Local congregation | Births, marriages, deaths, certificates of removal, disownments, disciplinary hearings |
| **Quarterly Meeting** | Region (several monthly meetings) | Minutes, oversight of monthly meetings |
| **Yearly Meeting (Philadelphia)** | Pennsylvania, NJ, and beyond | Policy minutes, epistles, oversight |

**What each record type gives you:**

- **Birth records** — Entries in meeting registers, often recording the child's name, parents' names, and date. Because Quakers did not baptize, these registers stand in for baptismal records.
- **Marriage records** — Uniquely rich. Quaker marriage required meeting approval and produced a **marriage certificate signed by every attendee** — a gold mine of related family names. Witnesses are often siblings, cousins, and neighbors.
- **Death records** — Entered in meeting registers; may include burial location.
- **Certificates of Removal** — Issued when a member transferred to another meeting. These are critical for tracing **migration routes**: the certificate names the individual or family, lists the originating meeting, and is countersigned by the receiving meeting. Follow the certificate trail to track families moving westward.
- **Disownments / Disciplinary Proceedings** — During the Revolutionary War, many Quakers were disowned for bearing arms or paying military taxes. A disownment entry confirms a person's Quaker membership and family, and may be the only record placing them in a specific meeting at a specific time.

---

### 2. Key Repositories

#### 🏛️ Friends Historical Library — Swarthmore College
**Swarthmore, Pennsylvania** | [www.swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library](https://www.swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library)
- **Largest collection of American Quaker records**, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)).
- Holds original monthly meeting minutes, registers, certificates of removal, and membership records for Pennsylvania and surrounding states.
- Access: on-site research; some finding aids online.

#### 🏛️ Quaker and Special Collections — Haverford College
**Haverford, Pennsylvania** | [www.haverford.edu/library/special-collections](https://www.haverford.edu/library/special-collections)
- Major second repository for Pennsylvania Friends records, with strong holdings for the Philadelphia area meetings.
- Access: on-site research; finding aids online.

#### 🏛️ FamilySearch (Online / Microfilm)
- **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800** — FamilySearch has digitized **1 volume (145 images, image group 001188322)** covering Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. ⚠️ **Browse-only**: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. You must page through image by image. Access at FamilySearch.org by searching for image group 001188322.
- FamilySearch has also **microfilmed many Pennsylvania monthly meeting minutes and registers**, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)). These are not all reflected as named collections in the current index — browse the Catalog at [FamilySearch.org/catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog) filtered to Pennsylvania and "Church Records" to find microfilm for specific meetings (e.g., Abington Monthly Meeting, Falls Monthly Meeting, etc.).
- **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** (Collection 1999196, 893,214 indexed records) — covers the period; useful for corroborating family relationships.
- **Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900** (Collection 1502909, ~199,000 records, no images) — overlaps the period; may include Quaker marriages compiled from meeting records.
- **Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950** (Collection 1571957, ~312,000 records) — overlaps; Pennsylvania recognized Quaker marriages as legally valid without a magistrate.

#### 🏛️ Pennsylvania State Archives
**Harrisburg, Pennsylvania** | [www.phmc.pa.gov/archives](https://www.phmc.pa.gov/archives)
- Holds colonial-era provincial records including early tax lists (excellent pre-1790 census substitute), land warrants, and court records. Not the primary repository for meeting records, but critical for contextual and corroborating sources.

#### 🏛️ Historical Society of Pennsylvania
**Philadelphia, Pennsylvania** | [hsp.org](https://hsp.org)
- Holds some Quaker-related manuscript collections; strong for Philadelphia-area families.

---

### 3. Published Finding Aid — Essential Starting Point

**William Wade Hinshaw, *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*, 6 volumes** — Abstracts meeting records from Pennsylvania and surrounding states. This is the standard index to start with before going to original records. ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)). Available in many genealogical libraries and partially digitized online (Internet Archive, Google Books). Search Hinshaw first to identify which monthly meeting a family belonged to, then pull original records for full context.

---

### 4. Corroborating Records (Non-Meeting Sources)

Since civil registration is absent for this period, pair meeting records with:

| Record Type | Coverage / Access |
|---|---|
| **Federal Census, 1790** | First federal enumeration; heads of household only. Available on Ancestry, FamilySearch, and Fold3. |
| **Pennsylvania Tax Lists (1769–1800s)** | Provincial/state tax assessments name adult male property holders — a substitute for pre-1790 census. At PA State Archives and FamilySearch microfilm. |
| **Land Records** — warrants, surveys, patents | Pre-1820 Penn proprietor records at PA State Archives and PA Land Office records; deeds at county courthouses. |
| **Probate Records** | County-level wills and administrations; FamilySearch collection 1999196 covers 1683–1994 (name-indexed). |
| **Court Records** | County quarter sessions and common pleas; useful for guardianships and land disputes involving Quakers. |
| **Revolutionary War records** | Many PA Quakers were disowned for service — confirm via meeting disownment records, then cross-reference NARA pension files (Fold3) if they later sought pensions. |

---

### 5. Research Quirks & Warnings

1. **No civil vital registration before 1906** — meeting records are the only systematic source of births, marriages, and deaths for Pennsylvania Quakers in this period. Do not search for a state birth or death certificate.

2. **Marriage certificates name all witnesses** — when you find a Quaker marriage record, extract every name on the certificate; these are often the extended family cluster and neighbors, giving a ready-made research list.

3. **Certificates of removal are migration trackers** — when a family disappears from one meeting, check whether a removal certificate was issued. The receiving meeting's records (even if in another state) will have the countersigned certificate. Families moving west often went through meetings in western PA, Ohio, or Indiana.

4. **Disownments during the Revolution are genealogically significant** — the minutes will identify the individual, their relationship to the meeting, and often family members who stood in their defense. This period (1776–1783) generated a surge of disownment entries.

5. **FamilySearch Yearly Meeting volume is browse-only** — the 145-image Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes volume (image group 001188322) has no name index and is not full-text searchable. Set aside time to read page by page.

6. **Cross the Delaware River into New Jersey** — Burlington Monthly Meeting (Burlington County, NJ) and other New Jersey meetings were deeply connected to Pennsylvania Friends. Families near the Delaware River routinely appear in both PA and NJ meeting records. Check the Friends Historical Library holdings for NJ meetings as well.

7. **Delaware (state) also applies** — Wilmington and other northern Delaware meetings were part of the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting network. A "Pennsylvania" Quaker family near the state line may have transferred to a Delaware meeting.

8. **Start with Hinshaw before original records** — the *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* abstracts are faster to search and will tell you which specific monthly meeting to target in the original microfilm.

9. **FamilySearch Catalog is broader than the collections index** — many microfilmed monthly meeting registers do not appear as named, searchable collections. Search the FamilySearch Catalog (catalog.familysearch.org) under Pennsylvania → [County] → Church Records to find browse-only microfilm reels for specific meetings.

---

### Summary: Where to Start

```
1. Search Hinshaw's Encyclopedia → identify the monthly meeting
2. Check Friends Historical Library (Swarthmore) for original registers
3. Browse FamilySearch Catalog for microfilm of that meeting
4. Read Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (FS image group 001188322) for 1750-1800
5. Pull PA Probate Records (FS collection 1999196) for estate and guardian records
6. Cross-reference 1790 federal census and PA tax lists for context
7. Check NJ / Delaware meeting records if near those borders
```

## Locality Guide: Pittsburgh (Allegheny County), Pennsylvania — Steel-Boom Era, c. 1870–1900

### Jurisdictional Context

**Allegheny County** was formed in 1788 from portions of Washington and Westmoreland counties. **Pittsburgh**, the county seat, was established in 1758 and became one of the world's foremost steel-producing centers by the 1870s. All record-keeping for this period is at the **county level** (Allegheny County) — Pittsburgh as a city generated no independent vital records registry.

Key boundary note: **no jurisdictional splits** affect the 1870–1900 window, but the neighboring City of Allegheny (across the Allegheny River, now Pittsburgh's North Side) was an independent municipality until 1907 and kept its own records.

> **Population note:** FamilySearch's population data tool returned no figures for Allegheny County — do not assume any specific count. Contemporary estimates place Pittsburgh's population around 86,000 in 1870, rising to roughly 321,000 by 1900, fueled almost entirely by industrial immigration.

---

### ① Industrial & Occupational Records *(Primary Focus)*

These are the records most specific to the steel-boom research question. They are the most fragmented but most distinctive source class.

| Source | What it contains | Where held | Access level |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Company employment records** | Worker names, start dates, departments, sometimes wages | **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh); **Rivers of Steel** archives (Homestead, PA) | Physical only — fragmentary; not digitized |
| **Union membership records** | Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel and Tin Workers locals; membership rolls, dues, grievances | Rivers of Steel archives; some at Heinz History Center | Physical only |
| **Pennsylvania State Factory Inspector Reports** | Annual reports listing factories, workforce counts by sex/age, accident reports by establishment | Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg); some digitized via HathiTrust | Physical / partial digitization |
| **Pittsburgh city directories** | Occupation, employer, home address — annual volumes from 1813 | **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** (strong run); some volumes digitized on Ancestry.com | Physical + partial digitization |
| **USGS / Sanborn fire insurance maps** | Mill and plant locations — useful for placing a worker geographically | Carnegie Library; Library of Congress online (LOC.gov) | Digitized (LOC) |

> **Quirk:** Company employment records were almost never preserved as a legal obligation. Carnegie Steel, Jones & Laughlin, and other firms discarded most personnel files. Treat survival as the exception, not the rule. City directories and union records are the more reliable occupational backbone.

---

### ② Vital Records

Pennsylvania **statewide** registration of births and deaths began in **1906**. However, **Allegheny County** began registering births and deaths at the county level from **1870** — earlier than the statewide mandate and a significant advantage for this research window. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Vital and Church Records":* [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records)*)*

| Record | Date range | Where held | FamilySearch collection | Access level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| County birth & death registrations | 1870–1905 (Allegheny Co.) | Allegheny County; PA State Archives | Check FamilySearch microfilm | Microfilm / physical |
| **Marriage licenses** | 1885–1950 | Allegheny County Courthouse | [Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) (ID: 1921317 — 524,189 records, 312,045 images) | **Indexed + images** |
| Civil marriages (broader) | 1677–1950 | Varies | [Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) (ID: 1571957 — 312,045 records, 156,023 images) | **Indexed + images** |
| Compiled marriages (index) | 1700–1900 | Varies | [Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) (ID: 1502909 — 198,765 records) | **Index only — no images** |
| Statewide death certificates | 1906–1968 | PA Dept. of Health / State Archives | [Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317) (ID: 2255317 — 4,218,763 records) | **Indexed + images** *(begins after target period — background context)* |

> **Quirk:** For deaths before 1870 — or births/deaths where county registration is incomplete — pivot to church burial and baptism registers (see §③ below). The 1906 statewide death certificates post-date the steel-boom era but are invaluable for an ancestor who died in retirement.

---

### ③ Church Records *(Critical for Ethnic Worker Families)*

The most important substitute for civil vital records and the primary family-data source for immigrant steel workers. Catholic parishes were organized along strict ethnic lines in Pittsburgh, each serving one community:

| Ethnic community | Denomination | Archive for original registers |
|---|---|---|
| Irish | Roman Catholic | **Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** |
| Slovak | Roman Catholic / Greek Catholic | Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives; Slovak Heritage Society |
| Polish | Roman Catholic | Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives |
| Croatian / Serbian | Roman Catholic / Eastern Orthodox | Catholic Diocese; Serbian Orthodox Diocese of Eastern America |
| Italian | Roman Catholic | Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives |
| German | Lutheran / Reformed / Catholic | Evangelical Lutheran Church archives; Catholic Diocese |
| Welsh / Scottish | Presbyterian | Presbyterian Historical Society (Philadelphia) |

> Parish baptism, marriage, and burial registers survive from the **1840s onward** for most Allegheny County Catholic parishes. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Vital and Church Records":* [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records)*)*

FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania church records — search the catalog at familysearch.org/search/catalog by county and denomination.

---

### ④ Census Records

| Census | Key fields for industrial research | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **1870 federal census** | Name, age, birthplace, occupation, real/personal property value | FamilySearch (indexed + images); Ancestry |
| **1880 federal census** | Name, age, birthplace, **parents' birthplaces**, occupation, relationship to head | FamilySearch (indexed + images); Ancestry |
| **1890 federal census** | ⚠️ **Largely destroyed nationwide** — do not assume it exists | N/A — see substitutes below |
| **1900 federal census** | Name, age, birthplace, parents' birthplaces, **immigration year**, **years in U.S.**, **months employed in year**, citizenship status | FamilySearch (indexed + images); Ancestry |
| **1880 Mortality Schedule** | Records deaths in the 12 months preceding June 1, 1880; includes cause of death — significant for mill accident victims | Ancestry; FamilySearch microfilm |

> **Quirk — 1890 gap:** City directories (Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh holds annual volumes), church records, and the **1892 Pennsylvania Soldiers' and Sailors' Home records** (for Civil War veterans) are the best bridges across this decade-long gap in census coverage.

> *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Census and Naturalization":* [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census)*)*

---

### ⑤ Naturalization Records

Mass immigration to Pittsburgh's steel mills generated a large body of naturalization records. Pre-1906, naturalization could be filed in **any court of record** — check multiple courts.

| Court / repository | Date range | Where held |
|---|---|---|
| Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas | 1798–1930 | **National Archives at Philadelphia** (701 Market St, Philadelphia, PA) |
| U.S. District Court for Western Pennsylvania | Various | National Archives at Philadelphia |
| Allegheny County Courthouse (originals) | Post-1906 | Allegheny County; USCIS genealogy program |

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Census and Naturalization":* [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)*)*

Also check Ancestry's Pennsylvania naturalization collections and FamilySearch's broader naturalization holdings.

---

### ⑥ Probate Records

| Collection | Date range | FamilySearch ID | Records | Images | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, Probate Records | 1683–1994 | [1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) | 893,214 | 446,607 | **Indexed + images** |

Wills and estate inventories from working-class steel families often list tools, machinery shares, or union benefit certificates — useful for occupational confirmation even for laborers who owned little real property.

---

### ⑦ Newspapers

Pittsburgh newspapers are an underused source for industrial-era genealogy: accident and fatality reports from mills, strike coverage listing workers, obituaries, and immigrant community notices.

| Resource | Notes | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Newspapers.com** | Large run of Pittsburgh Post-Gazette and other papers | [newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) — subscription |
| **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress) | Free; covers some Pennsylvania papers of the era | [chroniclingamerica.loc.gov](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | Microfilm runs of local papers | Physical |

---

### ⑧ Land, Property & Tax Records

City and county tax records (ward-level for Pittsburgh) document property ownership and — importantly — list **occupation** alongside assessed value. Deed indexes at the Allegheny County Recorder of Deeds Office. Some digitized on Ancestry.

---

### ⑨ Military Records

| Resource | Notes | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Civil War pension files | Many steel workers were veterans; pensions include biographical detail | NARA (Ancestry/Fold3 digitized) |
| Fold3 | Pennsylvania service records, pension index | [fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/) — subscription |

| Resource | Notes | Access |

| **Find A Grave** | Comprehensive for Pittsburgh-area cemeteries | [findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/) — free |
| **BillionGraves** | Secondary option | billiongraves.com |

### Top Research Quirks for Pittsburgh Steel-Era Families

1. **County vital registration started 1870** — Allegheny County preceded the 1906 statewide mandate; county-level birth and death records exist for the entire steel-boom period.
2. **1890 federal census is gone** — bridge the gap with annual city directories (Carnegie Library), church records, and the 1880/1900 censuses.
3. **Ethnic Catholic parishes are the backbone** — for Slovak, Polish, Croatian, and Italian steel workers, the Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives is often the *only* family record source predating naturalization.
4. **Company records are fragmentary by nature** — industrial personnel files were not a legal requirement; city directories and union records are the more reliable occupational backbone.
5. **Pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court** — search both Allegheny County Common Pleas *and* U.S. District Court records at NARA Philadelphia.
6. **The City of Allegheny** (now Pittsburgh's North Side) was a separate municipality until 1907 — ancestors living there generated records under Allegheny City, not Pittsburgh proper, through the end of the steel-boom era.
7. **FamilySearch wiki place pages** returned only generic content for Pennsylvania in this session — consult the Allegheny County-specific page directly: [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy)

# 📋 Locality Research Guide
## Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic (c. 1780–1820 window)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Philadelphia was chartered as both a **city and county** in 1682. In 1793 it was the capital of the United States, with a population of approximately **50,000**. The yellow fever epidemic ran **August–November 1793**, killing roughly **5,000 people** — about one-tenth of the city. Thousands more fled to the surrounding countryside, dispersing families across Chester, Montgomery, Delaware, and Bucks counties and into New Jersey. Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil registration** for births, marriages, or deaths in 1793; that did not begin until **1906**. Church records are therefore the primary vital source for this entire period.

*(Source: Wikipedia, "Yellow fever epidemic of 1793," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793)*

---

### ⭐ Epidemic-Specific Records (Highest Priority)

These are record classes that exist specifically because of the 1793 outbreak and are unavailable for most American research problems of the era.

| Record | What It Contains | Where Held | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mathew Carey, *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever*** (1793) | Contemporary published list of names of the dead; four editions by December 1793 | Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP); widely digitized | Physical + digital (Google Books / HathiTrust) |
| **Committee of Citizens Minutes & Reports** | Names of sick, dead, and relief recipients; appointed by Mayor Matthew Clarkson | Philadelphia City Archives; HSP | Physical; some transcripts published |
| **Bush Hill Hospital Records** | Patient records for the emergency epidemic hospital | HSP (manuscript collection) | Physical; check finding aids |
| **Benjamin Rush Papers** | Rush was the leading physician during the epidemic; patient notes and correspondence | American Philosophical Society (APS), Philadelphia | Physical; partially microfilmed |
| **Mayor Clarkson's Accounts** | Official documentation of epidemic response | Philadelphia City Archives | Physical |

*(Sources: FamilySearch Wiki, "Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever Epidemic of 1793," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793; Wikipedia, "Yellow fever epidemic of 1793," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793)*

---

### 1. Church Records (Baptisms, Marriages, Burials)

**Primary vital source for all of 1793.** Church registers are the only systematic recording of Philadelphia vital events before 1906. Burial registers from August–November 1793 will show a dramatic spike — this is your main tool for confirming epidemic deaths.

Key congregations active in 1793:

| Congregation | Record Type | Repository | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Christ Church** (Anglican/Episcopal) | Baptisms, marriages, burials | Christ Church Archives & HSP | One of the most complete colonial registers; burials spike in fall 1793 |
| **Gloria Dei (Old Swedes' Church)** | Baptisms, marriages, burials | Gloria Dei Archives & HSP | Oldest church in Pennsylvania (1698); Swedish Lutheran; covers waterfront neighborhoods |
| **St. Peter's Episcopal** | Burials, baptisms | HSP | Daughter church of Christ Church |
| **Mikveh Israel Congregation** | Burial records | Mikveh Israel Archives | Covers Philadelphia's Jewish community |
| **St. Mary's Catholic** | Baptisms, marriages, burials | Archives of the Archdiocese of Philadelphia | Significant Irish and German immigrant population |
| **German Reformed & Lutheran churches** | Baptisms, burials | HSP; FamilySearch microfilm | Large German community in Northern Liberties district |
| **Society of Friends (Quakers)** | Meeting minutes, birth/death registers | Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College; HSP | Quakers documented vital events meticulously and separately from civil authority |

The **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** (https://www.genpa.org) has compiled printed and manuscript indexes to many Philadelphia church registers and is an essential first stop.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)*

**FamilySearch coverage note:** `collections_search` returned no Philadelphia-specific church record collection. Check FamilySearch microfilm catalog directly for individual congregational registers (many were filmed in the mid-20th century). No digitized, indexed church record collection specific to 1790s Philadelphia was returned by the tools.

---

### 2. Census Records

| Census | Coverage | What to Look For |
|---|---|---|
| **1790 Federal Census** | Philadelphia city & county | Pre-epidemic household snapshot; establishes who was present before the outbreak |
| **1800 Federal Census** | Philadelphia city & county | Post-epidemic; missing heads of household from 1790 may reflect epidemic mortality or flight |

**Strategy:** Compare 1790 and 1800 enumerations for the same family. A household enumerated in 1790 that disappears entirely by 1800 (without an apparent move) warrants checking the church burial registers for fall 1793.

Ancestry.com holds the indexed U.S. Federal Census Collection (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/). FamilySearch also has the 1790 and 1800 censuses indexed and free.

---

### 3. Probate Records

FamilySearch holds **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** (Collection ID: 1999196, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196). This covers our 1793 period. Expect a **surge in probate filings for Philadelphia County in 1793–1794** as estates of epidemic victims were administered. Wills and estate inventories name heirs, creditors, and executors — often revealing family structure not captured anywhere else.

The **Philadelphia Register of Wills** (now the Philadelphia City Archives) holds the original volumes. County-level probate jurisdiction applies.

---

### 4. Civil Marriage Records

Two FamilySearch collections overlap the period:
- **Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950** (Collection ID: 1571957, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957)
- **Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900** (Collection ID: 1502909, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909)

**Caveat:** Marriage registration in Pennsylvania in 1793 was not systematically civil — the church record is the primary source. These compiled collections often derive from church transcripts and published abstracts; treat them as indexes pointing back to original church registers, not independent sources.

---

### 5. Land and Tax Records

Philadelphia's **city and county tax assessment lists** survive from the 1760s onward and are held at the **Philadelphia City Archives** and **HSP**. For epidemic research:
- A taxpayer on the 1793 list who disappears by 1794–1795 may have died or fled
- Property transfers recorded in **deed books** at the Philadelphia Recorder of Deeds (now Philadelphia City Archives) will reflect estate sales following epidemic deaths

The **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) holds some supplementary tax records and land warrant files.

---

### 6. Newspapers

Philadelphia's contemporary newspapers published **daily death lists** during the epidemic — an extraordinary genealogical resource unique to this event.

Key titles:
- *Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser* (Philadelphia)
- *Pennsylvania Gazette*
- *General Advertiser* (later renamed *Aurora*)

**Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com) and **Chronicling America** (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov, free via Library of Congress) hold digitized Philadelphia newspapers. Check issues from **August–November 1793** for death notices, departure announcements, and relief committee notices that name individuals.

---

### 7. Military Records

Many Philadelphia men served in the Continental Army or Pennsylvania militia (1775–1783), creating pension and service files a decade before the epidemic. For men who died in 1793, **bounty land warrant** files may name widows and heirs, establishing post-epidemic family composition.

- **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com) holds Revolutionary War pension and service records
- **NARA** (https://www.archives.gov) — originals at NARA I, Washington DC; pension files often contain rich biographical detail

---

### 8. Immigration Records

Philadelphia was a major port of entry throughout the colonial and early national period. For families whose origins are uncertain:
- **Pennsylvania, Naturalization Records** — filed in various courts of record (pre-1906 naturalizations not centralized)
- **Passenger lists** — NARA holds arriving passenger manifests; Ancestry.com has indexed the Philadelphia port arrivals

---

### 9. Cemetery Records

**Find A Grave** (https://www.findagrave.com) holds user-contributed cemetery transcriptions for Philadelphia-area burying grounds. Key 1793-era burial sites include:
- **Christ Church Burial Ground** (5th & Arch Streets) — Franklin is buried here; contains many 1793 victims
- **Gloria Dei Churchyard**
- **Ronaldson's Cemetery** (private, non-sectarian; opened 1827 — post-dates epidemic but holds later markers for families who survived)
- **Quaker burial grounds** (several locations)

Many epidemic burials were hastily performed in existing churchyards or in the **potter's field**; not all will have surviving markers.

---

### Key Repositories Summary

| Repository | Strengths for This Research | URL / Contact |
|---|---|---|
| **Philadelphia City Archives** | Official city records, Committee minutes, tax lists, deeds, Recorder of Wills | phila.gov/archives |
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** | Church transcripts, Carey list, Bush Hill records, Rush papers, newspapers | hsp.org |
| **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** | Indexes to church records, published abstracts | genpa.org |
| **American Philosophical Society (APS)** | Rush papers, scientific and civic correspondence from 1793 | amphilsoc.org |
| **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** | Quaker meeting records | swarthmore.edu/friends-historical-library |
| **FamilySearch** | Probate collection (1683–1994), compiled marriages, census; microfilm catalog | familysearch.org |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census, passenger lists, newspapers | ancestry.com |
| **NARA Philadelphia** | Federal court records (naturalizations), federal land, military pensions | archives.gov |
| **Library Company of Philadelphia** | Early printed Americana, Carey pamphlets, contemporary newspapers | librarycompany.org |

---

### Research Quirks & Cautions

1. **No civil vital registration in 1793.** Pennsylvania's statewide vital registration began in 1906. Church burial registers are the *only* systematic death record for the epidemic period — Pennsylvania did not register deaths at county or state level in 1793. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)*

2. **Thousands fled the city.** Families who evacuated to Chester, Montgomery, Delaware, or Bucks counties (PA), or across the Delaware River to Burlington or Gloucester counties (NJ), may have generated records — including deaths — in those jurisdictions, not in Philadelphia. Search neighboring county church records for fall 1793 if a Philadelphia ancestor goes missing.

3. **Death record vs. burial record gap.** Because epidemic burials were rushed and sometimes mass interments occurred, a person may appear on Mathew Carey's death list but not in a specific church burial register, and vice versa. Cross-reference all available lists rather than relying on any single source.

4. **Philadelphia City and County were coextensive** throughout this period, so records are filed under either "Philadelphia City" or "Philadelphia County" — treat them as one jurisdiction for record searches.

5. **FamilySearch death certificates (collection 2255317) begin in 1906**, 113 years after the epidemic. Do not search this collection for 1793 victims.

6. **The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania's published abstracts** of church records frequently contain errors introduced in transcription. Always verify against the original register or an image thereof.

---

### Recommended Starting Sequence

1. **Mathew Carey's 1793 list** — quickest confirmation of an epidemic death (HSP; HathiTrust digital)
2. **Committee of Citizens minutes** — for victims who received relief or were admitted to Bush Hill (Philadelphia City Archives / HSP)
3. **Church burial registers, Aug–Nov 1793** — for the formal burial record (Christ Church and Gloria Dei are the best-preserved; HSP for indexes)
4. **Philadelphia probate records, 1793–1795** — for estate administration naming heirs (FamilySearch collection 1999196; Philadelphia City Archives originals)
5. **1790 + 1800 Federal Census** — to bracket family composition before and after the epidemic (FamilySearch; Ancestry)
6. **Contemporary newspapers, Aug–Nov 1793** — for daily death notices and departure announcements (Newspapers.com; Chronicling America)

# Locality Guide: Chicago (Cook County), Illinois — Great Fire of 1871

**Jurisdiction:** Chicago, Cook County, Illinois, United States
**Target period:** c. 1860–1885 (spanning the fire and its immediate aftermath)
**Research challenge:** The Great Chicago Fire (October 8–10, 1871) destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and most locally-held pre-fire genealogical records. This guide leads you to what survived, what was reconstructed, and what exists for the post-fire period.

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Cook County was formed in 1831. Chicago incorporated as a town in 1833 and as a city in 1837. When the fire swept through on October 8–10, 1871, it destroyed approximately 3.3 square miles of the city, killed roughly 300 people, and left more than 100,000 residents homeless. The Cook County Courthouse — which housed deeds, birth and death registers, probate files, court records, and tax rolls — burned entirely. The Illinois General Assembly responded with the **Burnt Record Act of 1872**, which required property owners to re-register their deeds with the county.

**Key quirk:** Illinois did not begin *statewide* vital registration until 1916. Between the fire (1871) and 1916, vital records exist at the **Cook County level only**, not the state level. Before the fire, most civil vital records were also county-held and are now lost.

---

## The Record-Loss Problem — What Burned

The following were **destroyed** in the fire (largely unrecoverable at the county level):
- Pre-1871 deed books
- Pre-1871 birth and death registers
- Probate and estate files pre-1871
- Tax rolls pre-1871
- Most Cook County court files pre-1871
- Many individual parish church registers

---

## Record-by-Record Survey

### 1. Federal Census Records ✅ SURVIVED — Indexed + Images

**This is your single most important resource for pre-fire Chicago families.** The 1860 and **1870 federal censuses survived because the originals were stored in Washington, D.C., not in Chicago.** The **1870 census** is the last snapshot of Chicago's population before the fire.

- Available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.com (linked via curated external resources)
- The **1870 mortality schedule** captures deaths in the year prior to June 1870 — check it for any fire-adjacent deaths, though the fire postdates the 1870 census by one year
- The **1880 federal census** (also indexed, available on FamilySearch/Ancestry) captures where families resettled after the fire

> Source: [Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Record Loss and the Great Fire](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)

---

### 2. Cook County Vital Records (Post-Fire) — Indexed on FamilySearch

All three of the following FamilySearch indexed collections begin in **1871** — reflecting both the fire's destruction of earlier records and the county's post-fire registration system. They are your primary vital-record sources for families *after* the fire.

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Records | Date Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cook County Birth Certificates | 2024189 | ~1,450,000 | 1871–1940 |
| Cook County Death Records | 1913456 | ~980,000 | 1871–1947 |
| Cook County Marriage Records | 1756321 | ~620,000 | 1871–1920 |

> **Access:** Free at [FamilySearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org). Also linked via Ancestry.com.

---

### 3. Church Records — Pre- and Post-Fire ⚠️ Coverage Varies

Church registers are the **most important substitute for destroyed pre-fire vital records**. Parishes that survived the fire or were quickly re-established retained or reconstructed their registers.

**FamilySearch indexed collection:**
- **Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925** (Collection ID: 1803978) — ~285,000 records spanning both pre- and post-fire periods. This is the primary starting point.

**Physical repository:**
- **Archdiocese of Chicago — Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** holds Catholic parish registers. Contact required for access. Coverage varies by parish — some pre-fire registers were destroyed, others were salvaged or reconstructed.
- Individual Protestant, Lutheran, and other denominational archives hold their own series; access varies.

> ⚠️ **Gap warning:** Pre-fire church register coverage is uneven. Always check whether the specific parish existed before 1871 and whether its registers survived.

---

### 4. Property Records — Burnt Record Act Re-Recordings ⚠️ Partially Indexed

Two digitized volumes on FamilySearch are directly relevant to the fire:

**Volume 009982111 — Post-fire Property Re-recordings (1871–1880)**
- 112 images | **41% name-indexed** (searchable by name via FamilySearch record search for ~41% of entries; remainder must be browsed)
- Covers families who re-registered property under the Burnt Record Act of 1872
- ImageGroupNumber: 009982111

**Volume 009982110 — Pre-fire County Court Records (Reconstructed Copies, 1865–1871)**
- 38 images | **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable** → **BROWSE-ONLY**, image by image
- Reconstructed copies of pre-fire court records; must be reviewed page by page
- ImageGroupNumber: 009982110

> These two volumes together form one continuous property research trail across the fire divide — work both, despite their differing date labels.

---

### 5. City Directories — Critical Pre-Fire Substitute ✅ Survived

Chicago city directories from the **1840s onward survived the fire** and are held at the **Newberry Library** (Chicago). They record names, occupations, and addresses — essential for establishing where a family lived before and after the fire when vital records don't exist.

> Source: [Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Repositories](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories)

---

### 6. Insurance and Title Records — Key Property Substitute

The **Chicago Title and Trust Company collection**, held at the **Chicago History Museum**, contains insurance and title records documenting pre-fire property ownership. These are the primary substitute for the destroyed county deed books and are not available online — in-person or contact-requested access.

---

### 7. Newspapers — Fire Victim and Relief Lists

Historical Chicago newspapers are available via **[Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com)**. Post-fire editions of the *Chicago Tribune* and other papers published:
- Lists of dead and missing persons
- Property loss and claims notices
- Relief organization recipient lists

This is a highly underused source for identifying fire victims by name.

---

### 8. Military Records — Indexed Online

- **[Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)** — Civil War service records and pension files for Chicago-area men (subscription)
- **[National Archives (NARA)](https://www.archives.gov)** — Pension files, service records, and Civil War draft registrations; also holds pre-1906 federal naturalizations

---

### 9. Cemetery Records

- **[FindAGrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)** — Community-contributed transcriptions and photographs for Cook County cemeteries. Useful for post-fire death dates and surviving family connections.

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Holdings Relevant to 1871 Research | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Newberry Library** (Chicago) | City directories (1840s+), maps, manuscripts, pre-fire newspapers | In-person; some digitized |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Insurance/title records (Chicago Title & Trust), fire photographs, personal papers | In-person or contact |
| **IRAD — Northeastern Illinois University** | Cook County government records post-1871 | In-person |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers | Contact required |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records from 1871 onward | In-person or mail request |
| **FamilySearch.org** | 4 indexed Cook County collections + 2 digitized volumes (see above) | Free online |
| **NARA (Great Lakes Region, Chicago)** | Federal court records, pre-1906 naturalizations, federal census originals | In-person |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census, supplemental military and vital records | Subscription |

---

## Critical Research Quirks — Summary

1. **Start with the 1870 federal census.** It survived the fire intact and is your last pre-fire picture of Chicago families. The 1860 census is equally important for establishing origins.
2. **Pre-fire Cook County courthouse records are largely gone.** Expect gaps for births, deaths, deeds, and probate before October 1871. Do not assume a record existed and is merely undigitized.
3. **The Burnt Record Act of 1872** created a parallel re-registration trail. FamilySearch volume 009982111 (41% indexed) covers these re-recorded deeds 1871–1880 — always search this for property-owning families.
4. **Volume 009982110** (pre-fire reconstructed court records, 1865–1871) is **0% indexed and not full-text searchable** — it must be browsed image by image with no search capability.
5. **Church registers are the best pre-fire vital record substitute** — but coverage is uneven by parish. Always verify whether the specific parish and its registers survived.
6. **Chicago city directories at the Newberry Library** are indispensable for the 1840s–1870s. They are not fully digitized online and require in-person or reproductions.
7. **Post-fire newspapers** (available via Newspapers.com) published fire victim and relief lists by name — a frequently overlooked source.
8. **Illinois statewide vital registration did not begin until 1916.** Between 1871 and 1916, look for vital records at the Cook County level only; between the city's founding and 1871, the records are mostly gone.
9. **Insurance and title records at the Chicago History Museum** are the primary substitute for the destroyed deed books and are not available online.

---

## Recommended Research Sequence

1. **1870 and 1860 federal censuses** (FamilySearch/Ancestry) — establish the family pre-fire
2. **Church records** (FamilySearch collection 1803978; Bernardin Archives for Catholics) — pre-fire vitals
3. **Post-fire vital records** (FamilySearch collections 2024189, 1913456, 1756321) — births, deaths, marriages from 1871
4. **Burnt Record Act re-recordings** (FamilySearch volume 009982111) — property re-registration
5. **City directories** (Newberry Library) — address and occupation tracking across the fire
6. **Post-fire newspapers** (Newspapers.com) — victim and relief lists
7. **Chicago History Museum** — insurance/title records for property owners
8. **NARA** — naturalization and military records unaffected by the fire

# 🗺 Louisiana French Colonial Period (1700s) — Locality Research Guide

---

## Jurisdictional Context

The 1700s in Louisiana spans **two colonial regimes** with a transition around 1769 — a critical fact for every record search:

| Period | Regime | Language of Records |
|---|---|---|
| 1699–1769 | **French colonial Louisiana** — governed by the Superior Council (*Conseil Supérieur*) | French |
| 1769–1803 | **Spanish colonial Louisiana** — reorganized under Spanish colonial governance | Spanish (French continued in many church registers) |
| 1800–1803 | Briefly retroceded to France; then Louisiana Purchase (1803) | — |

France ceded western Louisiana to Spain in the Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762), but actual Spanish administration did not begin until 1769. The modern *state* of Louisiana was not admitted to the Union until 1812. *(Sources: Wikipedia — [French Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Louisiana); FamilySearch Wiki — [Louisiana Genealogy, French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))*

> **⚠️ Critical quirk — no civil parishes in the 1700s.** Civil parishes as known today were not established until ~1807 (Territory of Orleans era). Colonial administrative units were called *posts* or districts. Search by the Catholic ecclesiastical parish or colonial post name — not by a modern Louisiana parish.

---

## Record Types, Repositories, and Access

### 1. Catholic Parish Registers *(Primary Source)*

**What they contain:** Baptisms, marriages, and burials for the full population — free settlers, enslaved persons, and Indigenous people. The French *Code Noir* required Catholic baptism and recording of all enslaved persons, making these registers especially important for African-descended ancestry. St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans has registers beginning in **1720**.

**FamilySearch collection:** *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925* — [collection 1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) — covers the entire French and Spanish colonial period from 1718 onward.

> ⚠️ **Language:** French-period registers are in French; Spanish-period registers may be in Spanish or French. Period script (18th-century French cursive or Spanish script) requires specialized reading skills.

> ⚠️ **Indexing/browse status:** Volume-level search was not available in this environment — check the FamilySearch collection page directly to confirm whether records are name-indexed or browse-only.

**Physical repositories:** Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives; Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans).

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Louisiana Genealogy, French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))*

---

### 2. Superior Council (*Conseil Supérieur*) & Cabildo Records

**What they contain:** French colonial civil and legal records — land grants (*concessions*), court proceedings, notarized contracts, estate inventories, and wills. The Spanish-period equivalent is the Cabildo court records.

**Repository:** **Louisiana Historical Center, Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans** — partially digitized. Physical visit or copy requests likely required for full coverage.

> ⚠️ These are the primary civil and legal record source for the French colonial period and are essential for property, legal status, and family relationship evidence.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Louisiana Genealogy, French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))*

---

### 3. Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), France

**What they contain:** Administrative correspondence, census rolls (*recensements*), muster rolls, and colonial government records for French Louisiana. For the French colonial period especially, significant record classes exist **only in France**.

**Repository:** ANOM, Aix-en-Provence, France. Some records are accessible via the ANOM online portal. Records are in French.

> ⚠️ ANOM is indispensable for the French colonial period (1699–1769). No U.S. repository substitutes for it.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Louisiana Genealogy, French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))*

---

### 4. New Orleans Notarial Archives

**What they contain:** The oldest continuous notarial office in North America. Records from the **1730s** include contracts, marriage settlements (*contrats de mariage*), wills, property sales, and manumissions — often substituting for or supplementing parish register data.

**Repository:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center — public access, on-site.

> ⚠️ Records are in French pre-1769, and Spanish (sometimes French) post-1769.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Louisiana Land and Property, Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))*

---

### 5. Colonial Land Grants

**What they contain:** French concessions and Spanish land grants documenting land ownership and sometimes household composition.

**Repositories:**
- **American State Papers: Public Lands** — a published series available in major research libraries and digitized on HathiTrust; covers both French and Spanish grants confirmed by the U.S. government
- **Louisiana State Land Office**, Baton Rouge
- **Bureau of Land Management GLO Records** (glorecords.blm.gov) — for post-1803 patents

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Louisiana Land and Property, Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))*

---

### 6. Probate Records

**FamilySearch collection:** *Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984* — [collection 2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) — begins at 1756, covering the late French colonial and the entire Spanish colonial period.

> ⚠️ Pre-statehood probate records may be filed under the Superior Council (French era) or Spanish colonial court structures — not under the modern civil parish court system.

---

### 7. Colonial Census Rolls (*Recensements*)

**What they contain:** Periodic household-level counts naming heads of household, family members, enslaved persons, and livestock — invaluable substitutes for vital records.

**Repositories:** ANOM (Aix-en-Provence) for French-period counts. Spanish-period *padrones* may be at the Louisiana Historical Center or the **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain.

> ⚠️ No digitized FamilySearch volumes were confirmed for colonial census rolls in this environment — physical or microfilm research is likely required.

---

### 8. Spanish Colonial Records (1769–1803)

For the second half of the century, also consult:
- **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain — the primary repository for Spanish colonial administrative records for Louisiana
- **Papeles Procedentes de Cuba** (Papers from Cuba) — held at the Archivo General de Indias; covers Spanish Louisiana and is available on microfilm through several U.S. repositories

---

## FamilySearch Collections Confirmed for the Colonial Period

*(From `collections_search` — 4 total Louisiana collections; 2 overlap the 1700–1803 window)*

| Collection | Date Range | Colonial Coverage | FamilySearch URL |
|---|---|---|---|
| Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 | 1718–1925 | Full French & Spanish colonial from 1718 | [collection/1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) |
| Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 | 1756–1984 | Late French colonial + full Spanish colonial | [collection/2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) |

> The remaining 2 Louisiana collections (*Parish Marriages 1837–1957* and *Statewide Death Index 1819–1964*) begin after the colonial period and are not primary sources for 1700s research.

---

## Repository Quick-Reference

| Repository | Holdings for This Period | How to Access |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center, New Orleans | Superior Council, Cabildo, partial parish registers | On-site; partial digitization |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial contracts from 1730s | Public access, on-site |
| ANOM, Aix-en-Provence, France | Admin correspondence, census rolls, French colonial records | On-site + partial online portal |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial admin records (*Papeles de Cuba*) | On-site + microfilm via U.S. libraries |
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Church Records 1718–1925; Probate Records 1756–1984 | Free online |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | State-era + some colonial survivals | On-site |
| American State Papers: Public Lands | Colonial land grants confirmed post-1803 | HathiTrust (free online); major libraries |

---

## Key Research Quirks

1. **Two regimes, two languages.** The 1700s crosses the French/Spanish divide (~1769). Expect French records before 1769, Spanish after — but many Catholic parishes continued in French throughout. You must work in both languages.

2. **Code Noir & enslaved ancestors.** The French *Code Noir* mandated Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons and recording in parish registers. Baptismal registers are often the *only* genealogical record for enslaved African and African-descended families in this period.

3. **Essential French repository.** ANOM in France holds administrative and census records that do not exist in any U.S. repository. For the French colonial period, ANOM research is mandatory, not optional.

4. **Essential Spanish repository.** The *Papeles Procedentes de Cuba* at the Archivo General de Indias is the equivalent for Spanish Louisiana (1769–1803).

5. **No civil parishes yet.** Organize your search by Catholic ecclesiastical parish or colonial post, not by the modern civil parish system established in 1807.

6. **Notarial archives as a vital-records substitute.** Marriage contracts and wills in the Notarial Archives (from 1730s) frequently supply family data that supplements or replaces missing parish entries.

7. **External online databases have sparse colonial coverage.** The 6 FamilySearch-curated external links for Louisiana in this period are all generic U.S. resources (U.S. Census, NARA, Find A Grave, Newspapers.com, Fold3) — none are colonial-specific. Standard U.S. genealogy databases are largely unhelpful for pre-1803 Louisiana; archival and specialized repositories are essential.

| Records losses | Some colonial records were destroyed in fires and floods. The Louisiana Historical Center and ANOM finding aids are the best guides to what survives. |

**Suggested next steps:** If you have a specific family surname, post (e.g., Pointe Coupée, Natchitoches, New Orleans), or ancestral line in mind, a targeted research plan can sequence which of these record sets to search first and in what order.
